LESTER VS. BUTLER.

Motion by the United States Attorney to Dismiss the Actions.

NEW YORK, August 31.—The United States District Attorney this afternoon began the preparation of argument on the motion to dismiss certain actions now pending in the United States Circuit Court against General Benjamin F. Butler, to recover in all $475,000 damages. John H. Lester, now of New York, but formerly of Virginia, has two actions, one for $75,000 and the other for $100,000 damages. During the war it was discovered that Lester assisted in the manufacture of arms for the Confederate Government. He was tried by court martial and sentenced to ten years imprisonment with ball and chain, and his property was confiscated. Francis M. Fisk has an action for $300,000 damages for property, including machinery, molasses, household utensils, etc., confiscated by order of the President. A motion to dismiss will be made, on the ground that the defendant acted in accordance with a proclamation of the President in confiscating the property of plaintiff, and was therefore not liable to prosecution for damages.

Interesting Discovery.

The St. Petersburg correspondent of the London Standard reports that some interesting discoveries have been made at Kelver, where, in excavating ground for the new harbor, the hulls of several ships long buried in the earth, have been laid bare. Four Russian men of war, of considerable dimensions—120 to 180 feet long—have it, is said, been identified. From the inscription, "Olonets, 1711," on one of the cannons found, it seems that the ships were wrecked after that date, and the fact is curious, as showing how rapidly the water has receded. In old times the sea evidently came up to the walls of the town, which then must have presented a singularly picturesque appearance, with its quaint red-tiled houses, perched high on the rock above. At present there is half a mile of dry land between the walls and the harbor, and where great ships rode not very long ago the locomotive now runs between rows of wharves and merchants' offices.

Loss of Life from Lightning.

Loss of Life from Lightning.

CEDAR RAPIDS, August 31.—During a thunder storm this morning three barns, two dwellings and the fish hatchinghouse, in this immediate vicinity, were struck by lightning. CHEYENNE, March 23 — George Parrott alias "Big Nose George," one of the Elk Mountain murderers and an infamous road agent, who is under sentence to be hanged on April 2d, attempted to break jail this morning at Rawlins. He got his shackles off, with which he attacked Jailer Rankin when he entered the corridor to lock the prisoners in their cells for the night. The jailer's wife hearing the conflict had the presence of mind to lock the outside door, locking the Jailor in with the prisoners. An alarm was then raised and a large number of citizens hastened to the jail and released the Jailor and secured the prisoners. He will be doubly ironed and strongly guarded until the day of his execution. This action of George is surprising since he has always manifested a contrate spirit and did not desire a trial, pleading guilty to the indictment and desired to be hanged soon.

When the sentence of death was passed upon him he wept like a child, and broke down completely. He said his health was failing. In consequence these facts gained him much sympathy, but now threats of lynching are made, and all desire to see him suffer death.

Fears were entertained that, after all, this scourge might be again let loose on the community, and threats were made on all sides to anticipate the course of justice and invoke the potent presence of Judge Lynch. Groups of men met at various parts of the town and discussed the probabilities of the murderer succeeding in some one of his attempts to escape and thus cheat the gallows of its due. About half-past ten o'clock a party of masked men rode into town and the sound of hoof strokes aroused the deputies, who were on guard at the jail. Sheriff Rankin, anticipating some movement of this kind, was at the jail and was on the lookout for the nocturnal visitors. The latter, however, wasted no time in preliminaries, but at once demanded the keys of the prison. Before the Sheriff and his men could offer any material resistance they were overpowered and the masked deputies of Judge Lynch forced their way into the jail. Quickly proceeding to Parrott's cell they pinioned him and dragged him forth. The murderer, realizing that his hour had come, determined to die game and maintained a stolid demeanor to the last. He was taken to the railroad depot and a rope was flung over an arm of an adjoining telegraph pole. He was forced to climb up a ladder, and his last words were: "I will jump off, boys, and break my neck." No questions were put to him, as he had already confessed his crime. The noose was adjusted around his neck, and, at a signal, the ladder was pulled away at five minutes to 11. Leaving the body swaying in the air the entire party rode away, and the Elk Mountain murder was avenged.

ROLLA, Mo., March 23.—One of the boldest attempts at bank robbery in the history of Missouri occurred in this city at 3 o'clock this morning, which resulted in the death of the burglar, Pat Ebert. He arrived in Rolla about a month ago from Kansas, ostensibly looking for a location to open a saloon, taking up his lodging in a boarding house near the National Bank of Rolla. His suspicious conduct attracted the attention of the officers of the bank, who called to their aid Hank Devins, the City Marshal. Upon investigation it was discovered that the burglar had gained access to a vacant building adjoining the bank, and for three nights had been unmolestion to escape, and was shot down in his tracks. He lived one hour after being shot, but would reveal nothing. The Coroner's jury rendered a verdict of justifiable homicide.

PITTSBURG, Pa., March 25. — Two workmen on the Baltimore and Ohio road yesterday gave a wonderful evidence of their fidelity, deliberately choosing death to themselves in order to protect the lives of a hundred others who were in the care of the company. About half past 2 o'clock in the afternoon John Sullivan and his brother, Michael, were at work on the track, near Demmler station. John Sullivan was the section boss of the sub-division between McKeesport and Port Perry, and he had made a tour along the track to see if everything was in proper condition. He found a rail that was not quite straight, so he and his brother took a heavy trackman's crowbar and lifted the rail up to straighten it. While they were busily at work the afternoon accommodation train bound east with a heavy load of passengers came along. There was a curve just below the place where the men were working, and they did not see the train until it was almost upon them. They took in the situation at a glance. The rail which they had been fixing was lifted up and the huge crowbar was wedged tightly in such a position that the train would certainly be thrown from the track unless the bar was removed. On one side of the track was a hill and on the other a steep bank running down to the river, so if the train was thrown from the track while under a full headway of steam there would undoubtedly be an appalling loss of life. The men seized the bar and began frantically to pull and twist it about. The engineer of the train saw them, but could not stop. He says their efforts to free the crowbar and lower the rail were frantic and like the workings of madmen, and they seemed to forget their own danger. BIG-NOSED GEORGE.
Particulars of His Lynching at Rawlins. Wyoming--He is Taken From the Jail by Masked Men and Hanged to a Telegraph Pole.

Big-nosed George, alias George Parrott, who was sentenced to be hung in April for murder, made a desperate attempt to escape from the jail at Rawlins, a few days ago, and inflicted a dangerous wound on the head of the jailer, but he was finally secured.

The affair soon became generally known, and citizens of Rawlins assembled and proceeded to the jail, from which they took George and led him to a telegraph pole near the depot. A rope was thrown over the cross-arm and a noose was tied around the victim's neck. He was then made to mount a barrel, which was soon jerked from under him. This proved a failure, as he was only stunned, and he was cut down and, upon reviving sufficiently, he was ordered to climb a ladder, which was placed against the pole, and commanded to jump off. This he did, but the fall was not sufficient to break his neck. In his desperate struggles he got his hands loose, and, grabbing hold of the telegraph pole, he climbed up several feet, in the hope of easing himself and regaining breath. He got breath enough to speak, and begged piteously for some one to end his suffering with bullets; but no one seemed inclined to comply with his appeal. He soon became exhausted, and finally had to let go of the telegraph pole, and swinging out from it, he made a few kicks with each departing breath, and in a few minutes he died. The lynching was quietly conducted, and the coroner cut down the body and took charge of it.

Big-Nose George was one of the Elk Mountain gang of robbers who attempted to ditch and rob a Union Pacific express train, two or three years ago, near Medicine Bow, but were frustrated by the vigilance of a section hand, who discovered, just in time, that they had taken up a rail. They were followed to their hiding place by Tip Vincent and another deputy sheriff named Widdowfield, both of whom were discovered and killed by the robbers, who afterwards fled the country. Big-Nose George was captured in a mountain town a few months ago by a deputy United States marshal, to whom the desperado was given away by a woman with whom he (the desperado) was on intimate terms. A vehicle passed through the Black Hills recently with this motto:

"In God we trust;
Black Hills or bust."

The murder of Billy Bird on the 5th at Deadwood has not yet been solved, and it is very probable that it never will be.

In Nebraska they have it that Moses was an advocate of woman suffrage, because Miriam was permitted to lead the band.

The Denver Tribune still keeps at John Evans. If the libel suits win the paper will go in as about one-tenth payment.

Ogden shippers are reaping a harvest now in the vast quantities of produce they are sending out to supply less favored places.

The funeral of the late Joseph Young, of Salt Lake City, who died on the 16th inst., at the advanced age of 84 years, took place Tuesday.

Twenty-six bake shops now supply the people of Denver with bread. These twenty-six shops consume about one hundred sacks of flour daily.

Harvesting has commenced in the valleys in Dakota, and the prospects are that the yield will fall short of what was anticipated. by about one-third.

And still they come! Governor Evans wants $200,000 more from the Denver Tribune. Every new suit only causes friend Skiff to keep the closer to the vault.

Six incendiary fires have occurred at Portland, Orogon, within the last two days. The police believe there is a gang of burglars organized to commit arson and plunder.

L. L. Paddock made a fist attack on the editor of the Boulder Herald a few days ago, and the latter accuses the former of striking like a schoolboy and spitting like a cat.

Mrs. Robert Rankin, of Rawlins, has been presented with a gold watch as a testimonial for her bravery and heroic action in preventing the escape of Big Nosed George last spring.

A party of Italians are examining California localities in Northern Sonoro county, with a view of purchasing several thousand acres of land, intending to set out the largest vineyard in the state.

A man suffering from hydrophobia was locked up in the Fort Collins calaboose on the 18th, the officer thinking him drunk. Upon ascertaining the facts the man was turned loose, and disappeared.

The waterspout at El Paso, New Mexico, last week, damaged city property to the amount of $50,000. Southern Pacific railroad property $8,000, and washed away a bridge of the Atchison, Topeka & Santa Fe railroad.

Thirteen hydraulic mining companies have applied to the board of equalization of Nevada county, California, for a reduction in their assessments, on the ground that pending litigation and the judicial injunction laid upon them renders their property of much less value.

A smelting works employe named Shultz was a victim of sunstroke on Wednesday evening in Omaha. While walking he fell unconscious on Ninth street, and was taken home in a hack and put under the care of a physician. He was much better yesterday, and will recover.

A mill for the manufacture of corn goods, grits and corn flour is being built at Omaha on Eighth street, near the Omaha elevator, by Mr. Latham Davis. It is to be a frame structure. It is an experiment, and if the enterprise proves successful a much larger mill will be put up.

The Virginia Enterprise says that at the C. & C. shaft a great amount of electricity is generated by the cables running over the sheaves or by the machinery generally, as of nights a ball of light constantly hovers about the top of the railing. This constantly gives off sparks, with a loud snapping noise. There is probably enough electricity going to waste to light up the works, if properly utilized.

JUST PUNISHMENT.
A Brutal Negro Lynched at Marianna, Arkansas.
Little Rock Democrat, 13th.]
Morgan particulars are
Little Rock Democrat, 13th.]
Meager particulars are being received in this city of a terrible occurrence, with a tragic termination, at Marianna, Lee county, Saturday last. A colored man, named Dave Ramsey, met the daughter of one of the county officials in the suburbs of the town, and attempted to ruin her honor. The cries of the girl, who is only twelve years of age, attracted attention, and the fiend was frightened away before accomplishing his hellish design. She told the story of the assault to her father, who informed his friends, and the whole town turned out in pursuit of the brute, who was quickly captured, hung to the nearest tree and his body riddled with bullets.

LITTLE ROCK, Ark., Jan. 13. On Tuesday the daughter of Sheriff C. H. Banks, of Marianna, Lee county, was brutally outraged by a negro, who was captured and lodged in jail. An infuriated mob surrounded the prison, overpowered the guards and, taking the darkey out, literally riddled his body with bullets.
black-prisoner-mariana-1881-01-12.A6:
LATE NEWS ITEMS.
A number of delegations of colored men have waited upon Gen. Garfield at Mentor, urging the claims of their race in the general distribution of offices under the new Administration, and especially the propriety and justice of placing a representative colored man in the Cabinet. Senator Bruce is the gentleman most prominently named in connection with a Cabinet position.

H. W. OLIVER received the Republican caucus nomination for United States Senator from Pennsylvania. He was supported by the Camerons. A number of Republican members refused to enter the caucus, and a bolt was apprehended.

THOMAS C. PLATT received the Republican caucus nomination for United States Senator from New York—another triumph for Senator Conkling.

McMILLAN is the successful candidate for United States Senator from Minnesota.

GOVERNOR CHURCHILL, of Arkansas, was formally inaugurated on the 13th.

SECRETARY SHERMAN is of the opinion that we can not float a three-per-cent bond.

GOVERNOR FOSTER of Ohio denies the rumor that his withdrawal from the Senatorial contest was in pursuance of an understanding with Garfield and Sherman that the latter should resign and enter the Cabinet, and he (Foster) succeed to the Senate. He says there has been no understanding whatever about the matter.

PARNELL will ask for a select committee of the House of Commons to inquire into the outrages in Ireland.

The defense in the Land League trials opened on the 13th. McDonough denounced the prosecution as a landlords' indictment against the tenants of Ireland. The courtroom was crowded.

A NEGRO was shot to death by a body of citizens near Marianna, Lee County, Ark., for committing a most horrible assault upon the daughter of Sheriff Banks.

HARRIS M. PLAISTED was inaugurated Governor of Maine on the 13th.

HON. R. H. STEPHENSON, for fourteen years Collector of Customs at Cincinnati, is dead.

THOMAS J. KIRK, a well-known hardware merchant of Chicago, committed suicide on account of business troubles.

A FIRE at Trenton, Tenn, on the night of the 12th, destroyed the Herald office, the Hicks House, and several other business houses. A number of persons were injured.

In the Senate, on the 13th, the Army Appropriation bill was further considered. The House spent the day in Committee over the Funding bill.

A fire at Weatherford, Texas, caused the loss of $35,000. Partially insured.

The Meriden house burned at Meriden, Conn., Jan. 12. Loss probably $50,000; insurance, $45,000.

Robert McQuaig, financial secretary and treasurer of the Planters' Union, Chicago, has run away with all funds of the concern.

A passenger car on the Wabash express was ditched in Illinois and a number of passengers severely, though not fatally injured.

Mrs. Alice Williams, of Kent county Mich., a devout Catholic, while suffering from temporary aberration, cut her tongue nearly out with a razor, as a sacrifice to the Lord. She's in a critical condition.

PERSONAL.
Rev. Robert Matlock, a preacher reported to have been lynched by a mob in the Boston mountains, in Arkansas, some six months ago, it seems was not lynched, as he was recently seen near Corsicana, in this state. Matlock was the starter of a new religion, a sort of mixture of all creeds, and soon had a crazy following about him. In his fanaticism he denounced all who would not think as he did, and was particularly severe on a family named Miller. Finally one of the family, a young man about 20 years old, told him he must stop his abuse of his family or take the consequences. Thus ill feelings arose between them, which culminated in their meeting one day at a public gathering where they talked the matter over and agreed to forgive and forget their differences and shook hands on it. As young Miller turned away, after they had taken awhile, Matlock suddenly drew a long knife and cut Miller's throat, severing his head nearly from his body. The excitement was tremendous, and an indignant crowd went in pursuit of the fleeing Matlock, and, as he was not seen afterwards, it was concluded he was caught and hung.

Governor Crittenden, of Missouri, has offered a reward of $100 for the arrest of Louis Merrick, charged with the murder of James Maupin in Chariton county, that
Rev. Dr. George B. Russell has accepted the presidency of Palatine college, at Myerstown, Pennsylvania. He was formerly pastor of Washington mission, of the Reformed church in the United States.

Mr. Boehwer, aged 83 years, and for thirty years a prominent citizen of Brookville, Indiana, while hunting eggs in his hay loft, a few days ago, fell through a hatchway, and was instantly killed.

Ira Harris, not unknown in Dallas as receiver of the Dallas & Wichita railroad at one time, is one of the corporators of the new enterprise, "the Thor Ironworks," just starting in Kansas City.

Mr. James Gordon Bennett, of the New York Herald, has taken a party of friends to the Yorktown centennial in his own yacht, and they will live on board of her while there.

Judge Scofield, of the United States court of claims, has returned to Washington city after a considerable absence, recuperating his health during the summer months.

Ex-Senator Spencer, from Alabama, under the carpet-bag regime, is now in Washington city, and it is said he will be given a good position under the new government.

Miss Ida McCreary, first lady assistant in the public schools of Carbondale, Illinois, died, a few days ago, her death creating the profoundest sorrow among all classes.

G. E. Whitney, a prominent contractor on the Fort Wayne railroad, was run over by a freight car and killed at Hamlet station on that road a few days ago.

The senator for Ain, France, Monsieur Bonnet, in jumping a ditch recently, fell and broke both his legs. He was out gunning at the time.

Ex-Governor Routt, of Colorado, it is said, has been recommended by General Grant for postmaster-general when Mr. James retires.

Mr. and Mrs. Ferdinand Jones, of Chicago, who have spent some years in Europe, will spend the winter in Washington city.

The wife and children of Assistant Secretary of State Hitt are visiting the mother of Mrs. Hitt, at LaFayette, Indiana.

Henry Garfield, son of the late president, has been elected vice president of the freshman class at Williams college.

The mother of United States Senator Sewell is dangerously ill at her home in New Jersey.

Hon. A. G. Thurman, ex-United States senator from Ohio, has arrived home from Europe.
The life of General Burnside is to be written by Ben Perly Poore.

WASHINGTON, October 7th — The Senators
The Situation at the National Capital.

WASHINGTON, October 7th.—The Senators of both parties to-night are averse to being interviewed as to what they will or may do in the organization of the Senate. There is a sentiment of concession on both sides, but no Senator knows just how far it will go, and he does not like to express an opinion which may embarrass him when he come to vote. It is freely admitted that there must be some concession and compromise, but what shape it will take cannot be foretold. Some suggest that a President pro tem, be elected for the express purpose of swearing in the new Senators, his term of office to be until next year, and after that an organization can be effected. There are precedents for this. The Senate has in the past elected a President for a specific duty or for a designated period of time. On one occasion a President was elected for one day. There are at least three Democratic Senators who are in favor of conceding the President to the Republicans if they will accord to the Democrats the Secretaryship and half of the committees, and let the remainder of the organization stand as now. One of the most influential Democrats in the Senate to-night expressed himself in favor of this plan. He said he was satisfied that if the Democrats would accord the President to the Republicans, an amicable agreement can be reached in a short time, and the Senate organized by a unanimous vote; but if, on the other hand, the Democrats take advantage of their temporary majority to elect a President he believed the Republicans would fight on the question of Secretary, and the remainder of the organization to the last day of the Forty-seventh Congress. This Senator said that if another deadlock arises it will run, there is no telling how long, and will block legislation at the regular session of Congress. This would be ill-timed and disgraceful, said this Senator; therefore he considered that the easiest and best plan is to give the Republicans the office they most desire, which is President of the Senate. A conference committee will be appointed by both caucuses to-morrow, and the prevailing belief is that those committees will arrange a plan for organization which will be accepted by both parties if the Republicans will divide the committees with the Democrats to gain the President of the Senate. It is not improbable that this plan will be adopted, as naturally there are a number of Democrats who would like to get their former committees again. There is considerable speculating as to how Senator Davis, of Illinois, will vote nothing to indicate what
ber of Democrats who would like to get their former committees again. There is considerable speculating as to how Senator Davis, of Illinois, will vote, but nothing to indicate what he will do has yet been heard from him here. He will reach here to morrow.

At the beginning of the last special session of the Senate, when the contest over the organization was just opening, it was announced to the Democratic caucus, by the authority of Senator Davis, that he proposed voting for a Democratic organization. Judge Davis declined to filibuster, but said he would vote with the Democrats. Subsequently, after the Republicans obtained the committees, in a speech he said he thought the organization should go with the committees; but notwithstanding this opinion he voted with the Democrat, except upon dilatory motions. The Democrats here express confidence that he will vote with them this time, unless they should take some position calculated to bring about a deadlock.

The President and the Pastors.

WASHINGTON, October 7th.—The pastors of this city, accompanied by the Maryland Lutheran Synod, in session here, called on President Arthur this afternoon at his residence. Dr. Chester, pastor of the Metropolitan Presbyterian Church, was spokesman for the visitors, and read the address. The President responded substantially as follows: "I am glad to meet you, gentlemen, yet it is with deep sorrow, under circumstances which have sadly devolved such momentous duties upon me. In the performance of these duties, as chief of a God-fearing and religious people, I appreciate my dependence upon their moral support and approval and upon the Divine blessing and guidance. I thank you cordially for the assurances of your support, for your kind expressions of sympathy and confidence." At the conclusion of President Arthur's response the visitors were individually introduced and shook hands with the President. The party then retired, evidently much pleased with the interview.

The Senate Secretaryship.

WASHINGTON, October 7th.—A canvass of the Republican Senators shows a great lack of earnestness upon the question of Secretary, and there are several who say that if Democrats secure the presiding officer they might as well take all the Senate offices. This state of indifference is said to be due to Gorham's candidacy as the caucus nominee, and if he could be induced to withdraw the Republicans could undoubtedly secure the Secretaryship. He absolutely declines to withdraw, in a paragraph in the Republican of this morning.

Train Robbers Plead Gullity.

LITTLE ROCK (Ark.), October 7th. — Cox, Stephens and Delaney, the Iron Mountain train robbers, pleaded guilty in the Hempstead Circuit Court to-day, and were sentenced to the penitentiary for terms of twenty years each.

National and International Garfield Memorial Hospital.

WASHINGTON, October 7th. — Senator Miller has been appointed on the Executive Committee for the establishment in Washington of a national and international Garfield memorial hospital, to the erection of which he asks popular subscriptions in any sum, from not only the people of the United States but from the world at large.

War Among the Authors.

NEW YORK, October 7th. — Joaquin Miller writes in reply to McKee Rankin's claim to having written "The Danites," and paid the poet merely for the use of his name: "The books which have borne my name were executed by patient toil. They have elicited from reviewers many severe criticisms. I have been charged, and perhaps justly, with many faults and follies; but the charge of want of originality is not one of them. In the 10,000 pages of comment upon me and my works, I have yet to find the accusation that I received the honor and the pay for the task performed by another. When, therefore, a man like McKee Rankin makes a charge of this kind, I find myself in the position of one who, when about to sit down to his boiled joint, finds that a dog has stolen it, has munched it out of palatable shape, rolled it in the mire, and claiming proprietorship. The exact result of such an incident is that morally the joint is the man's, but actually when he comes to look at it he doesn't care to own it, or to engage in a canine fight to prove that he ever did."

Dan Smith, a Negro Monster.
Makes a Brutal Assault
Upon a Girl Twelve
Years of Age.
His Arrest and Narrow Escape from the Righteous Wrath of the People.
outrage on the person of a little white girl living on Shoal creek, in this county, near the Alabama line. The circumstances under which the crime was committed are of the most cruel and revolting character and well calculated to excite the ungovernable fury of the people. The victim, Mattie Hendricks, is only twelve years of age and the treatment she received at the hands of this atrocious monster is almost too horrible to describe. She lives in the family of Elder William Smith and the outrage was committed when that gentleman and his wife were absent; the unfortunate child being the only person in the house at the time. Her story is about as follows: She was sitting indoors knitting, when the negro, who had lived on the farm all his life, entered and immediately grasped her by the arm, attempting at the same time to place his hand over her mouth. She screamed and attempted to release herself, when he caught her by the throat, lifted her up bodily and carried her out of the house, crossing a foot-log over the creek into a thicket where he subjected her to every indignity that his beastly propensities could suggest. The poor child lost consciousness while being carried across the foot-log and did not recover it until the ravisher had fled. She then dragged herself, with great difficulty, to the house, falling three times on the way, and enduring intense pain. She had been choked so cruelly and persistently that the blood ran out of her eyes, nose and mouth. Her mind, too, was flighty, and it was only at intervals that she knew where she was or what she was doing. She was discovered in this condition late in
servals that she knew where she was or what she was doing. She was discovered in this condition late in the evening by a gentleman who had occasion to stop at the house. Medical investigation showed that while her body had been terribly injured the negro wretch had not fully accomplished his purpose. In a few hours her throat was so dreadfully swollen and inflamed that the surface was on a level with her chin, and her other injuries were of such a character that for awhile her life was despaired of. Skillful treatment, however, had its effect and it is now thought that she will recover.

Of course this inhuman and revolting crime excited the most intense indignation among the people of the neighborhood and several parties of men scoured the woods in search of the negro. He managed to elude their vigilance in some way and was not arrested until Sunday, when he was discovered at Rogersville, Ala., and recognized by a description that had been sent to the authorities there. At first he denied his name, but when confronted by a gentleman who knew him, he saw that a lie would no longer serve him and he made a clean breast of the crime. He was immediately sent under guard to this place, the party traveling all night and reaching here early Monday morning, when the brute was turned over to Sheriff Arrowsmith. That official, impressed with a sense of duty, immediately put him on the morning train for the purpose of carrying him to Nashville for safe-keeping.

This becoming known, dispatches were sent to Lynnville, and when the train arrived at that place the negro was taken from the custody of a special deputy while the sheriff, who had stepped on the platform, was conversing with a friend. Mr. Arrowsmith, as soon as he discovered this fact, went in search of the prisoner and found him several hundred yards down the track in the custody of several men. Drawing his pistol he demanded that the negro be returned to him, and after a short parley he succeeded in obtaining possession of him and bringing him to Pulaski that evening. In the meantime, dispatches were sent to Prospect, the nearest point to the scene of the outrage, informing the people of the negro's return, and it was soon understood that a party of armed men would immediateley set out for Pulaski to wreak vengeance on the brute. The feeling was almost universal that the wrath of the people should be allowed to take its course, and a report that the girl was dead fanned the flames of popular fury. At about 1 o'clock that night about one hundred men rode into town and halted in front of the jail. Several of them dismounted and went in where they found Capt. F. Arrowsmith, brother of the sheriff. Demanding the keys, they were surrendered, but a visit to all the cells revealed the fact that the negro had been removed. Very naturally, the nocturnal visitors were very indignant, but they offered no violence, and the most of them rode quietly out of town. Sheriff Arrowsmith, moved by a high sense of official duty, which the better judgment of his fellow-citizens must ultimately approve, however much they may deprecate its effect in allowing a brutal ravisher to escape swift and condign punishment, had taken the negro from the jail, put him in charge of Deputy John W. Dyer and Special Deputy R. A. F. Jackson, with instructions to convey him to Nashville over land. These gentlemen, by taking a circuitous route, made the journey through the country without being molested, and succeeded in reaching Nashville Tuesday evening with the prisoner. INDIGNATION MEETING.
Action of the Citizens of the Southern Part of the County in the Rape Case.
Action of the Citizens of the Southern Part of the County in the Rape Case.

A meeting of the citizens of South Giles county was held in the school house near Thompson's mill on Friday, 15th inst.

On motion of Dr. M. S. Waters, J. C. Potts was called to the chair and J. P. Jones made secretary.

By request of the chair, Dr. M. S. Waters stated the object of the meeting to be a general consultation of the people, whereby steps might be taken, in order that justice might be promptly satisfied in the case of Dan Smith, colored, who committed an outrage on the person of Mattie Hendricks a few days since.

After considerable discussion, which was participated in by a number of those present, it was decided to send a memorial to Sheriff Arrowsmith.

On motion of M. W. Roberts, M. S. Waters, I. W. Anderson, Mack Currey, J. M. Howard, J. P. Jones and O. C. Jones were appointed a committee to draft said petition.

The committee reported the following:

NEAR THOMPSON'S MILL,
SOUTH GILES COUNTY,
Oct. 15, 1880.

To H. ARROWSMITH, SH'FF.

We, the citizens of South Giles county, have met to day in council, and have arrived at this conclusion:

That your course in the defense of one Dan Smith, colored, has been of such an extreme as knows no parallel, and is unwarranted by law, in our deliberate and candid judgment.

Now, we must, and do insist, that said Dan Smith, colored, shall be returned to Pulaski for trial, (as promised by yourself), that justice may be met, and that speedily.

We further agree and pledge our selves that we will not in any way molest, or cause said Dan Smith, colored, to be molested, until the court shall have assembled which shallin vestigate his cause.

We further feel that the dignity of law, the character of state, and the safety of our wives and daughters demand this, and should you find it in your heart to ignore these appeals, we denounce you as unworthy of our confidence.

Written in coolness, but never the less in sternness.

As to your action in this matter we request that you give the committee bearing this petition a written answer immediately.

With kind regards, we have the honor to be

YOUR OBEDIENT SERVANTS.

This petition was signed by all the meeting and a number of other substantial citizens, representing the bone and sinew of our land.

On motion it was ordered that a committee of twenty-five should be appointed to wait on Sheriff Arrowsmith and present this petition and receive his reply.

By request of the chair, Dr. Waters appointed the following named gentlemen as said committee: J. P. Jones, W. J. Blassingim, A. J. White, J. M. Howard, F. T. Petty, S. W. Gladish, J. S. Brownlow, J. A. L. Jones, O. C. Jones, C. E. Barnett, R. J. Barnett, A. C. Thompson, R. A. Sherrell, Sidney Locke, M. W. Roberts, Billie Davis, W. J. Hammonds, J. M. McConico, Mack Currey, J. C. Potts, Thos. Nance, W. S. Hopkins, H. T. Mitchell, J. S. Grant and W. C. McRee.

On motion the meeting adjourned until 3 o'clock next day, at which time the committee was ordered to report.

The committee met in Pulaski on Saturday morning, 16th inst., about 9 o'clock. Maj. Stacy kindly tendered the Chancery court room, in which to transact its business. The roll was called, and the committee all present except O. C. Jones and Billie Davis. The latter was represented by proxy, John Case. Dr. Waters being present, was chosen to fill the vacancy occasioned by the absence of Mr. Jones.

Mr. Arrowsmith appeared before the committee, and, after hearing the petition read, asked for a little time to consult before replying, which was granted.

The following was Sheriff Arrowsmith's answer:

In response to your communication, I say that I will use every effort in my power to bring Dan Smith to the speediest trial that can be had under the law, either at a special term, or at the next term in November, now four weeks off, and I will bring him promptly to the jail in Giles county, on the assurances in your petition, and I further request that you appoint one or more of your committee to go with me to Nashville to bring him back. Respectfully,

Oct.16. H. Arrowsmith, Sheriff.

The committee appointed W. J. Blassingim to go with the sheriff to Nashville, and returned and found quite a concourse of people awaiting the sheriff's answer. When it was read they quietly dispersed, seeming to be satisfied.

In justice to Mr. O. C. Jones we state that his absence from the committee was not on account of any disposition on his part to shirk a public duty, but was owing to the sickness of a very valuable horse, which demanded his personal attention. J. C. Ports, Ch'm.

J. P. Jones, Sec'y.

THE NEGRO RAVISHER.
Some Unexpected and Perplexing Difficulties Cropping Out in His Case.
The only event of considerable interest that is likely to transpire in Circuit Court now sitting is the bringing in of the indictment against and the arraignment of Dan Smith, the Shoal creek fiend. Smith is still in the Nashville jail, where he was taken by the sheriff to prevent the insenced people of the vicinity in which he attempted his helmish deed from visiting their wrath upon him summarily. Judge McLemore, as appears from his charge to the grand jury, upholds Sheriff Arrowsmith in his action of removing Smith to Nashville. The question of absorbing interest now is, will Smith be brought here at this term for trial? It cannot be answered yet. It is reported that the witnesses against him will not appear at this term; because they think if they do not appear and no indictment is found, he will be brought to Pulaski and released and will then be out of the sheriff's hands and can be dealt with as he deserves. We do not believe this report. If the witnesses do not apear and no indictment is found, he will be released in Nashville, if at all, and then he will be out of reach. He will not be brought here, as we understand, until the indictment is lodged, and until the witnesses apear the grand jury can find no bill, of course. It depends, therefore, upon the promptness of the witnesses to appear before the grand jury as to whether or not he will be brought here. We urge them to come. The complaint has been that the courts are too tardy in such matters, but if action like this is taken by the witnesses the blame cannot be laid there. Smith ought to be tried speedily and punished severely. Sheriff Arrowsmith did what he conceived to be his duty in running him off, and now he proposes to do as he is directed by the court. Judge McLemore approves his action, but will, unless prevented, see that the law is administered swiftly and surely.

It is useless to conceal the fact that grave apprehensions are entered here that Smith will be taken upon his arrival and hanged by the infuriated people of the country in which the crime was committed. We counsel against this, not on his account, for he more than deserves it; but the court is sitting with every appliance ready for his speedy punishment, and if the law proposes to throw off its tardiness for once and act swiftly, the people should lend it their aid. It is use less to mince words here, however. The people demand Smith's trial and punishment. If they are delayed for any reason, the consequences may be terrible. If they are hastened, we believe the people will allow the law to take its course. Following is the charge of Judge McLemore to the grand jury last Monday upon this point:

I deem it my duty to make a few remarks to the public. I have heretofore had occasion to publicly remark that you had had, since my acquaintance with the county, good sheriffs, and good jurors, and consequently that all guilty men had been punished according to law. But since the last term of my court here, I am informed that the sheriff of your county has had to rescue a prisoner from the hands of a mob determined to hang him, and to send him to another county for safe-keeeping.

What I wish to say is, that mob-law is a remedy for nothing and an aggregation of all evils. In a civilized, law abiding community, like yours has always been, it is an abomination on the face of the earth. There are only three lawful modes of taking human life. One is, in self-defense, when your own life is in imminent peril. Another is, to prevent an atrocious crime, such as rape or murder, when a party is in the act of perpetrating such crime. The other is, when the executioner hangs a man for crime, after indictment, lawful trial and sentence by a competent court.

Now, I am informed that many of the men engaged in this affair are good men and ordinarily law-abiding men, and that they severely censure the sheriff for his action in the premises. Instead of blaming the sheriff you ought to thank him. If the man had been hung, every man engaged in the hanging would have been, in contemplation of law, committing murder. One crime, however dark, does not justify another crime. When the sober, second thought shall return, every upright, honest man engaged in that affair will be thankful that the coolness of the sheriff prevailed over the heated excitement of the crowd. The sheriff simply did his duty and ought to be commended for it by all good men everywhere. The courts are open and Giles county juries have never yet failed to do their duty.

PRAIRIE DU CHIEN HOTEL BURNED.

[Special Telegram to the Globe.]

McGREGOR, Dec. 2.—The Mondell house, Prairie du Chien, VanVelser, proprietor, was burned this morning. Insured, house $5,000; furniture $1,000.

STORE BURNED IN EAU CLAIRE.

MILWAUKEE, Dec. 2.—The store of T. F. Malone in Eau Claire burned this morning. Loss $15,000; partially insured.

A DUEL THWARTED.

BUFFALO, Dec. 2.—A duel which was to have been fought between Lawrence Trimble and John Benton, of Covington, Ky., was thwarted by the non-appearance of Benton. Trimble, accompanied by W. N. Ward, also of Covington, was at Niagara Falls today, but the Benton party didn't arrive.

A RAVISHER HUNG BY A MOB.

NASHVILLE, Tenn., Dec. 2.—Dan Smith, colored, who attempted to ravish a young white girl in Giles county, some time ago, was sentenced to twenty-one years in the penitentiary, at Pulaski, for assault with intent to commit murder. As soon as the verdict was found a mob rushed into the court room, overpowered the sheriff and posse, seized Smith and dragged him to the street, where hundreds of people joined the mob, took him to a bridge and hung him until dead. The mob came from the vicinity where the crime was committed by Smith.

AN ABSCONDING BROKER CAUGHT.

CLEVELAND, O., Dec. 2. — Upon a telegram from Oil City giving a description, the police here to-night arrested a man giving the name of Joseph A. Johns. On searching him $5,700 was found, and a mark on his shirt showed his name to be Kennett McLeod. Subsequent dispatches represented him as an Oil City broker who had obtained $5,550 from Reynolds & Co., bankers of Oil City, by false pretenses, and also charges him with conspiracy. His family lives in Canada, where he was bound.

FIRE IN TOPEKA.

TOPEKA, Kan., Dec. 2. — Crawford's Opera House, which was opened last September, was burned this morning. Loss about $80,000. Insured for $15,000 in the German and Queen's, American Central, New York, Hamburg, British American, Union, of California, National, of Hartford, and St. Paul. Lovejoy's auction store and three other establishments on the ground floor were ruined, but the loss is not yet ascertained.
dan-smith-pulaski-1880-12.A10:
PULASKI.
Dan Smith, the Kavisher, Hanged By a Mob.
Regular Corr. of the Banner.1
PULASKI. TENN. December
PULASK, TENN., December 2. — Smith, the ravisher, arrived to-day from Nashville on the south-bound train, at two o'clock. A jury was empanelled and the submitted his case, and the extreme penalty of the law in this case was given him—twentv-one years in the state prison. There was quite a crowd in town, and as soon as it was known that he was here, four taps on the court house bell called the crowd together, and they went in the court room and took the prisoner therefrom and proceeded to the bridge across Richmond creek, in the south end of town, and hung him to one of the roof trestles until he was dead. I did not witness the affair, but from what I can gather it was orderly conducted. No one was masked, and the crowd was composed of many of the best men in the county. Everybody to-day says amen to the execution, as Smith's crime was one of the most brutal ever committed in this country. He caught the poor girl by the hair of the head and dragged her two or three hundred yards, even dragging her through a creek. He choked and beat her in a most unmerciful manner, leaving her for dead. He, however, did not accomplish his hellish intentions. We of Giles county are a law-abiding people, but all such deeds as that of Dan Smith will certainly meet with death, be the perpetrator black or white. The unfortunate girl has about recovered from her injuries.
dan-smith-pulaski-1880-12.A13:
A NECKSECUTION.
The Appropriate Ending of a Lecherous Villain.
PULASKI, Dec. 2. — Dan Smith, the negro who ravished a little white girl, Mattie Hendricks, on Oct 11, in the second district of Giles county, was taken from the court-house here to-day and lynched. He had been previously removed to Nashville to protect him against violence. He was brought down on the 1:30 train and carried to the courthouse, where he was immediately tried. He plead guilty to the charge and was sentenced to twenty-one years' imprisonment in the penitentiary—the extreme penalty of the law. Smith was heard to complain at the severity of the punishment.

The sheriff intended to return with him to Nashville on the 2:15 train. News of the trial becoming noised abroad, a mob of 800 to 1,000 men quickly collected, and although the sheriff and his posse offered a determined resistance, they were overpowered and the mob took the prisoner away determined to administer justice at their own hands. They carried him down Main street to the bridge that spans the romantic Richland creek. A rope, one end of which was tied around Smith's neck, was fastened to a beam of the bridge. Rev. Wm. Smith, the man who raised Dan, got into the wagon and prayed for him. The preacher also raised the victim of the negro's devilish design. While Mr. Smith was talking one man cried out, "This man dies for the safety of the whole people." The affair was a terrible one, but no more so than the fiendish deed for which he was executed. The affair occupied a very few minutes.
dan-smith-pulaski-1880-12.A14:
THAT INDICTMENT.
Six of the Grand Jurors Explain the Delay in Bringing it In.
PULASKI, Dec. 4, 1880.

EDITORS CITIZEN:—We, the undersigned Grand Jurors, desire to make a statement through the columns of your paper in reference to the indictment of Dan Smith, col'd, who was hanged by a mob at Pulaski on Thursday last.

The witnesses for the state appeared before us on the first Thursday of the court and their testimony was reduced to writing; but the indictment which had been proposed by the Attorney General was purposely held back from us, in opposition to our wishes often expressed both to the Judge and Attorney General, until Thursday morning the 3rd inst., when the indictment was found and returned into court.

Some of us desired prompt action in the case on account of the excitement in the public mind, and informed the judge that the public would be disposed to censure us for our delay, but he very promptly and decidedly informed us that he would bear the responsibility of our delay in bringing in the indictment.

We feel that it is due to ourselves, that we make this explanation of our conduct to the public.

E. F. AYMETT,
J. W. McGILL,
J. F. HANNA,
JAMES McLEAN,
S. E. S. MATTHEWS,
W. W. RUTLEDGE.

THE SMITH-FULKERSON MEETING.—The following account from an eye-witness of the meeting at Abingdon between Senator C. T. Smith and Fulkerson, is taken from the Lynchburg Virginian. [We omit most of the epithets used.]

Mr. Smith, seeing Colonel Fulkerson standing on the opposite side of the street, with other citizens, walked across, saying as he did so, "That is Fulkerson, the —" Mr. Fulkerson drew his pistol. Mr. Smith, continuing, said: "You have said you would cane me on sight, and I have come to give you a chance to do so. You have your cane, and now is your opportunity."

Colonel Fulkerson, who had levelled his pistol at Mr. Smith (who was then close at hand), said, "If you advance further or raise your hand, I shoot you."

Mr. Smith promptly raised both hands and stood full front to Colonel Fulkerson, and, placing them on his own breast, said to Colonel Fulkerson in a ridiculing manner, "You ——, you would not shoot a cat"; and advancing a step or so, added, "You have always plead your shattered arm as an excuse for not fighting. Now, I will tie one arm behind me, and we will fight it out."

Colonel Fulkerson replied, "I have not done so, but I will not fight that way; and I have denounced you in the press as a coward."

"Yes," said Mr. Smith, "after I had so denounced you face to face, and so proved you in the press." Bystanders, by words, tried to stop the difficulty. Mr. Smith said, advancing, and Colonel Fulkerson still pointing his pistol at him: "As you have said I was a coward who would not fight, and you refuse to fight now, or to shoot, I will fight you as a gentleman should fight."

Colonel Fulkerson replied: "Get your pistol and let us fight it out here."

Mr. Smith, who had not attempted to draw his pistol before, as he walked away, drew it and said: "There is my pistol and I have others, but I will not engage in a street-fight, as that is no evidence of courage, but of rowdyism. But I will, to end this matter, fight a duel with you, and will send or accept a challenge."

Colonel Fulkerson said: "I will not fight a duel at all."

"Then," said Mr. Smith, "I am done with you," and he went away.

Our informant says the town was much excited over this close approach to a serious matter.

Both parties were arrested and fined $1 each, but were not bound over to keep the peace.

"Dr." MILLER GONE.—Dr. Miller, the magnetic healer left for Harrisonburg on Monday last. While here he treated over seven hundred persons for all sorts of diseases. He made no charge whatever and more than half of his patients paid nothing. His receipts we learn were between $300 and $400. Some of those treated were benefitted, whether permanently or not remains to be seen. The "Doctor," whatever else he may be, is no fraud. He pays his own expenses, charges his patients nothing and if they want to pay anything will not receive more than a small sum from any one person. In some cases marked relief followed his treatment and in others he made a total failure. He is now at Harrisonburg.—[Staunton Vindicator.

A DEFENSE FOR THE BIBLE.—Dr. Talmage preached Sunday on Ingersolism vs. Christianity. He said he had no nervous anxiety about the overthrow of Christianity. He spoke of the Bible as the book of which 250,000,000 copies have been printed—the book that adorns the centre table, that is found at the bench of justice, and is placed in the trunk of the young man just leaving his country home for the city. There were four objections made to the Bible by infidels: It is an impure book, a cruel book, an unscientific book, full of laceration, manslaughter and massacre. Dr. Talmage asked: "How many of your acquaintances have learned cruel habits from reading the Bible? Do your children learn from the Bible to tear off the wings of more flies or to pin more grasshoppers, or to rob more bird nests? Oh, sirs, when you make a rose leaf stab like a bayonet, when you can manufacture icicles out of the south winds, when you can poison the tongue from a blossom of buckwheat, then you can find cruelty gotten out of the Bible." As to the alleged unscientific character of the Bible Dr. Talmage said: "My friends, who told you that there was an unbridgable gulf between science and the Bible? You hear the names of Mill, Darwin, Tyndall, Renan. I can give you names of men higher than those, as Mount Washington and the Himilayas are higher than the Ridgewood reservoir. There were Herschel, Kepler, Liebnitz, Ross and Isaac Newton. At the time Voltaire said that the story of the dissolving of the golden calf was impossible, there were at least fifty shops in Paris when gold was held in solution. When there is an apparent discrepancy between science and the Bible, all that is necessary is to wait."[—N. Y. Sun.

A DRUNKEN WOMAN'S TERRIBLE CRIME.

A fearful tragedy took place in the western part of Toronto, Canada, last week, two children, aged five months and three years respectively, having fallen a sacrifice to the desperate recklessness of a drunken mother. The woman's name is Annie Casey, wife of James Casey, a lumberman. Mrs. Casey had been drinking heavily of late. On Wednesday evening a sister of Mr. Casey saw her, and she had the children safely in bed. On Thursday morning the sister-in-law went into the house and found the two children dead, and the mother in a state of stapefaction from drink. In one corner of the room were signs of an extinguished fire with a broken lamp. A gin bottle and a dead cat were lying on the charred and blackened floor. The mother gave a rambling and senseless account of having upset the lamp and set fire to the room, causing her children's terrible death. She said she had extinguished the flames, but they caught fire again. One of the babies was apparently badly burned, its skin being blistered and reddened from head to foot. The woman was arrested.

Mrs. Casey died in the hospital on the 3rd inst.

A Desperate Darky Crossed the River of Death.
Ed Neims, the Murderer of Kufu Armistead, Meets his Just Reward.
river, opposite the foot of Jackson street, about half past one o'clock last night, by Chief of Police W. C. Davis.
The circumstances leading up to this point are as follows. Between nine and ten o'clock last night the Chief was informed that Nelms was in the city, and had made arrangements to be taken across the river in a skiff at midnight.
Without loss of time a party was made up, and headed by the Chief, went across the river in a skiff, landing at the Teenie Vance place, just above the old government light. They waited in a laborer's cabin near the bank for some time, watching for the skiff, but it failed to arrive when expected, and the entire party, with the exception of the Chief and Captain Hackett, returned to the city, believing they were on the wrong scent. The Chief declared his intention of remaining all night, and arranged with the balance of the party to fire his gun at daylight as a signal for them to come for him. The Chief and Captain Hackett took turns at watching. At half past one o'clock, while the Chief was on the look out he
HEARD THE SOUND OF OARS and discerned the dim outlines of a skiff rapidly approaching the bank. Dashing back to the cabin Captain Hackett was warned, and a laborer named A. Bodkins, who was present, was requested to go along and be ready to disarm the criminal in case he should surrender without resistance. The trio stole softly down toward the bank, which was sloping at this point, and stopped behind a log, about forty yards from the water's edge. Captain Hackett and Bodkins stooped behind the log, but the Chief, who discovered they had been seen, threw aside all reserve, and called out:
“Halloo, boys! Got any whisky aboard?”
“Who are you?” demanded one of the party.
“Oh, we're working for the railroad!” the Chief answered; and then asked:
“Where are you from?”
“Across the river,” was the answer.
“And where are you going to?” was again asked.
“We want to make out toward the railroad,” was the reply.
The Chief fearing the skiff party would recognize his voice, requested Bodkins to do the talking. That gentleman told the party they could not get out through the course they were pointing, but had better come near to where they were, as that was the best way to the high road. The party, four in number, walked up the bank, making directly for the spot where the officers stood. When they had approached within ten feet of him, Chief Davis presented his gun at the head of Riley, the uncle of Nelms, who was carrying a shotgun, and apparently was the only one of them armed.
“Surrender,” he cried, “or you are a dead man; I am an officer of the law.”
“I surrender,” said Riley, dropping the breech of the gun to the ground.
At this instant the Chief's eye detected one of the party who he at once thought to be Nelms, slipping his right hand around to his hip and at the same moment was startled to learn that Captain Hackett's gun covered the same man his did, and that Nelms was left uncovered. Swinging his gun around so as to bear on the murderer, he commanded him to surrender. Nelms never uttered a word, but crouching himself close to the ground, began slowly walking backward, with his hand still creeping toward his pistol, and his eyes staring fixedly into those of Chief Davis. The latter reiterated his demand, when Nelms suddenly stepped forward. Mr. Davis had advanced upon Nelms as the latter had retreated, and was within a few yards of him at the moment. He was not quite certain that it was the man he wanted, the shadows of the night.

PREVENTING HIM FROM BEING RECOGNIZED,

but he felt sure enough of it to be satisfied that there was no time to lose. He pulled trigger, thinking to cripple his man, but the load of shot lodged square into the side of Nelm's head, near the temple, ranging diagonally backward, and he fell dead. The other two men, who were unarmed, quietly surrendered.

Nelms' body was picked up and a navy six found clutched in his hand, the weapon lying under his body, he having fallen forward upon his face. It was a close call for Chief of Police Davis, and he did not act too promptly. The dead man was taken up and laid in the skiff, and within ten minutes after landing, the entire party were on their way back to the city. The inanimate body now lies in a plain pine coffin in the courtyard of the city prison. An inquest will be held later. Riley, Nelms' uncle, is in the calaboose and talks freely. He says Nelms came to the city by the back

SOLD HIS FARM.

Some days ago the father of the dead murderer sold his farm, a quarter section of land situated two miles from the river, near Norfolk, in Desoto county, Miss. The purchaser was Mr. J. T. La Prade, a popular citizen of Star Landing, and on Thursday last that gentleman paid its former owner $560 in cash for the realty subject to a previous mortgage upon it. Nelms' father went down the river from this city last Tuesday to close up his interests in the old homestead.

Mr. W. H. Rawlings, an officer connected with the jail at Senatobia, arrived in the city this morning and identified the body of Nelms. Jim Riley arrested at the time Nelms was killed, is the latter's uncle by marriage. He claims that he had been advised of Nelms' probable coming some days ago, and he expected him to arrive by the M. & C. railway.

At the time Nelms escaped from the Senatobia prison a few nights since, four other prisoners got away. One named Jim Morris, col'd, was recaptured and returned to his former quarters. Morris was under a charge of horse stealing. Another of the escaped prisoners named Lewis Flower, charged with petty larceny, was also retaken here a day or two since. It was from these that Captain Davis ascertained, or surmised, that Nelms would be harbored in this city, perhaps by his mother, who lives at the house of a Mr. Bacon, on Alabama street, in the southern part of the city.

One of the colored jurors who served at the time Nelms was last convicted, called at the station house.
NELMS' CRIME
was the killing of Mr. Rufus Armistead, manager on the plantation of Mr. Ed Hart, fourteen miles south of this city, on the evening of May 9th, 1880. The act was committed about 8 o'clock, just after dark. While Armistead was on his way from the stock lot to the house, Nelms, from an ambush, shot him just as he passed through the gate, the load tearing his stomach fearfully, and causing death in a few hours. Armistead had not done injury to Nelms, and indeed did not know him. Nelms had been employed by Mr. Hart in person that very day to do farm work, and had hardly spoken to Armistead. He evidently hired himself to Mr. Hart, with the intention of killing Armistead, as it was proven in trial that he had said he would have the blood of an Armistead if he had to kill a child to accomplish his end.

Nelms escaped at the time, but was subsequently captured in the cane brakes of Tunica county, after having been closely pursued for several days by dogs and men. He was in a half-starved condition and pretty well fagged out when taken. Several colored men who harbored Nelms in that vicinity were afterwards murdered by unknown persons, said to have been masked at the time, and the story is current that two of the slaughtered men were tied to the backs of their animals, with their stomachs upward, and their bowels were ripped open with butcher-knives. The perpetrators of these alleged diabolical acts have never been brought to justice.

After Nelm's arrest he was tried, convicted, and sentenced to be hung His case was appealed to the Supreme Court, which tribunal remanded it for a new trial. At the second trial he was again convicted and sentenced. The day arrived for his execution, and when the morning of it came, a telegram from Jackson, Miss., announced that the Supreme Court had again interfered, causing a stay of proceedings and a postponement of the hanging until the technicalities of the trial could be decided on.

Meantime the friends of Nelms busied themselves in his favor, and a few weeks ago his jailer awoke to find that he and four other prisoners had escaped in the darkness of the night, while he slumbered and dreamed.

INQUEST.

Equire Quigley held an inquest at 11 o'clock on the body of Nelms. Nearly an hour was occupied in hearing testimony, the following witnesses being examined: Captain Pat Hackett, Isaac Riley, A. Bodkin, Chief W. C. Davis, John Armistead and W. H. Rollins, jailer of DeSoto county, Mississippi. Their testimony was substantially the same as published.

This negro had killed Mr. Rufus Armistead, manager on the plantation of Mr. Ed Hart, which is located several miles south of Memphis, on May 9, 1880. The cowardly ruffian shot Armistead from an ambush while he was passing from a stock lot to the house. It was proven at the inquest that Armistead did not know Nelms personally, but that the latter had a grudge against him for having shot his brother in self-defense. He hired himself to Hart, it is said, for the express purpose of getting even with Armistead. When he had committed the cruel murder he immediately fled.

ARMED BANDS OF MEN
pursued him, and the hunt was one of the most exciting in the history of crime. The negro kept up the struggle for several days, hounded down by dogs and men. He ran from forest to forest, brake to brake, and seemed to have a charmed life. Finally he was captured in the canebrakes of Tunica county by officers. He was then the stag at bay, but was taken nevertheless. So great was the hatred of the negro, that several persons who harbored him were found mysteriously killed and no clue to the perpetrators. Some of the murdered men are said to have been horribly mutilated, and the evil ones have never been punished therefor.

SENTENCED TO DEATH.
Nelms was tried for the killing, and sentenced to be hung. The case was taken to the Supreme Court, and remanded for a new trial. The negro was again tried, and was found guilty, and sentenced to be hung. On the day of the execution the Supreme Court again interfered and stayed the proceedings. While awaiting for a decision by the court the jail was broken, and Nelms escaped. As several of the prisoners came to Memphis, it was thought highly probable that Nelms had came to this city also; the fact that he had relatives here made it still more probable. The police here have been upon the alert to capture him.

CHIEF DAVIS'S MIDNIGHT TRIP.

A great may people may not know it, but Memphis has a chief of police who hardly knows what fear is. Chief Davis is one of the most modest and conscientious of men, loved by all the officers on the force; and with all these qualities that endear, he is resolute and unfinching as a lion. Naturally he wanted to secure the arrest of Nelms if he were in Memphis, and out of this desire grew one of the most exciting and dangerous examples of police work on
rally he wanted to secure the arrest of Nelms if he were in Memphis, and out of this desire grew one of the most exciting and dangerous examples of police work on record. The Chief was informed by a certain person that he had overheard a negro named Riley bargaining with two other negroes to row him across the river at midnight. This Riley is an uncle of Nelms, and the supposition naturally was that he intended having Nelms taken over to Arkansas. The Chief and Captain Hackett got a party together and prepared to cross the river in order to receive Nelms. Not knowing where he would start to cross from, they concluded that it would be better to be on the other side.

The officers crossed in a skiff, landing just above the old Government light, and taking up their stand in a laborer's cabin near the bank, they watched for some time, but the skiff did not put in appearance, and so everybody left but the Chief and Captain Hackett, and a railroad hand named A. Bodkins, who was asked to go with them and disarm the negro if he did not resist. Until half-past 1 o'clock there was no sign of anybody, but at that time a skiff was faintly apparent gliding.

OVER THE DARK RIVER toward the shore. The Chief, who was on watch, notified Captain Hackett and Bodkins, and all of them went quietly down to the bank. The negroes in the boat saw them, and the Chief called out boldly: "Hello, boys! Have you got any whisky with you?" The men in the boat wanted to know who they were. The Chief said they were railroad hands, and wanted to know where they were bound to. The negroes said they wanted to get over toward the railroad. Bodkins then, at the Chief's request, told the negroes they had better land there as it was the best place along the bank; and the skiff was accordingly pointed toward the shore, and the men disembarked.

like the wild beast he is, was prepared again to kill. The Chief's attention was attracted to him by his panther-like attitude and the movement to get his pistol, so he quickly pointed his gun at him and commanded him to surrender. The dead murderer's body was taken to the skiff and carried across the river to this city, where it was turned over to the relatives of the deceased, who yesterday morning put it in a pine coffin. Nelms came to Memphis Wednesday morning and put up at his mother's house at Fort Pickering. The relatives of Armistead and officers from Senatebia identified Nelms. The former embraced Chief Davis when they saw the murderer dead.

CAPTAIN DAVIS
is of course very sorry that he had to kill the negro, but it was simply unavoidable, and he has the sympathy of the community. Nelms was no better than a dog, and his taking off was only anticipated a few days. There will be none to regret him. CRIMINAL NEWS.
Gathered from Various Portions of the Country.
CHATTANOOGA, TENN, December 28.
—A special to the Times gives an account of a terrible tragedy which occurred this morning at Bellefont, Ala., a small station on the Memphis and Charleston Railroad. 44 miles from this city, resulting in the probable fatal shooting of C. M. Feerel. W. D. Martin aud his son John. They are the only merchants in the place, and the difficulty originated in jealousy. The weapons used were pistols.

MACON, GA., December 28.—At R. und Oak, Jones County, 40 miles from here, a young former named Jack Wm. Gray, interfered with a negro dance Monday night, and was fatally stabbed by three negro brothers, Bob. Henry and Alex. Jackson. Gray fired into the brothers, killing all three, one dying on the spot, one before reaching the door, and the other a few hours later. Gray crawled out of the house and died on the steps.

ATLANTA, December 27.—Yesterday, at Debray, in Upson County, a general fight occurred, in which Dock Wilson killed Ed. Johnson, his half-brother, and Brad Garland killed A. P. Harris. The fight was with knives. There was a murder committed at the same town some weeks ago.

TODAY, General Wm. McRae, superintendent of the Western and Atlantic Railroad, resigned, and Robert Anderson was elected to fill the vacancy. Joseph M. Brown, son of Senator Brown has been made general freight agent.

Elijah Whitehead was killed by Turner Sutton, at Hawkinsville, Pulaski County, yesterday. Both were negroes.

NEW ORLEANS, December 28. — Mrs. M. F. Cappage was killed last night by the accidental discharge of a pistol with which her oldest child was playing. She had been instructing the child how to aim the weapon, and sat down on the floor to play, when the child aimed the pistol and fired, the ball entering her brain. No one knew that the pistol was loaded.

MEMPHIS, TENN., December 28. — Ed. Helms, a negro murderer, who, with six others, recently escaped from the Hernando (Miss.) jail, was killed this morning by Chief of Police W. C. Davis. Helms, with three others, were making for the Arkansas shore, when they were intercepted by Chief Davis, with Captains Hackett and Oliver, also of the police force. When Helms was commanded to halt, he endeavored to shoot, but his gun missed fire. Chief Davis then fired with fatal effect. Helms and his party were wellarmed with shot-guns and pistols. His companions were captured and lodged in the station house.

CINCINNATI, O., December 29. — A special from Gore, Ohio, says the authorities placed a guard about the house of Mrs. Terrell, who was assassinated last night to prevent the obliteration of the tracks of the assassin. As soon as daylight came they traced the assassin to the residence of Mr. Arnold, a farmer, and arrested Morgan Richard, one of Arnold's farm hands, as the criminal. He was armed with revolvers which had one empty chamber. He resisted arrest, but was overpowered and placed in a wagon and driven rapidly to Logan to jail, barely escaping lynching. No motive for the crime has been discovered. Norfolk, December 28.—Information has been recieved of a threatening riot at Plymouth, N. C.

SHOT BY POLICE.
An Escaped Negro Convict Killed.
MEMPHIS, December 29.—Ed. Nelms, the negro murderer, who, with six others, recently escaped from the Hernando, Miss., jail, was killed this morning by Chief of Police W. C. Davis. Nelms, with three others, was making for the Arkansas shore, when they were intercepted by Chief Davis, with Captains Hackett and O'Hara, also of the police force. When Nelms was commanded to halt he endeavored to shoot, but his gun missed fire. Chief Davis then fired with fatal effect. Nelms and his party were well armed with shot guns and pistols. His companions were captured and lodged in the station house.

The Legislative Council met yesterday afternoon, with President Padden in the chair, and Messrs. Burke, Graves, James Lee, jr., James, Kney and Wallace present. The following report was made by the engineer:

ENGINEER'S REPORT.

"In relation to the petition of the Springfield and Memphis Railroad Company asking the Taxing-District to share one-third of the cost of a culvert which they propose to build in the bayou on Broadway street, in the Tenth ward, in constructing their line from Fifth street to a connection with the Mississippi and Tennessee railroad near Alabama, I submit herewith, as directed by your resolution, a plan and approximate estimate. It is proposed to build a six-foot arch one hundred feet long, the full width of the street, with parapet well twenty-four feet long carried up three feet above the grade of the street. The estimate of a brick-arch culvert is $2266, and the estimate of a stone-arch culvert $3520. MILES MERIWETHER."

Referred to the Board of Public Works.

The engineer recommended that in the matter of Ike A. Chase, asking to be allowed to lay a plank walk in front of his residence on Alabama street, and to have lamp removed from its present location, the petition be granted and the lamp ordered removed. Adopted to sidewalk and lamp to be removed, provided Chase pay expense thereof.

A petition was received calling attention to the horrible condition of the sidewalks on the west side of Dunlap street from Poplar street to Lane avenue, and asking that the sidewalks be repaired, and that a few gas or oil lamps be put up. Ordered laid.

PETITIONS.

A petition was received asking that a plank crossing be made over Third street, on each side of Poplar. Referred to engineer to lay crossing.

A petition was received from the pupils of Miss Higbee's high school stating that it is necessary for most of them in order to reach the schoolhouse to cross Beale and Lauderdale streets, or one of them; that almost any rain produces mud enough to cover their shoes and render their feet damp, and frequently their clothes are soiled in crossing the street; that it appears to them that a small expenditure of money would remedy this very great inconvenience and very much promote their comfort. They conclude as follows: "Feeling assured that your honorable body will be disposed to grant any reasonable request we may make, we respectfully ask that substantial crossings, sufficient to keep us out of the mud, be placed across each Beale and Landerdale streets, and that the same be down with as little delay as possible."

Referred to the engineer, with power to act.

A petition for a sidewalk on Mosby street, between Hill street and Winchester avenue, was received and the sidewalk ordered laid.

A petition for a sidewalk on the west side of Main street, from Beale to Pontotoc, was received, and the sidewalk ordered laid and repaired with brick.

The petition of Montgomery Anderson to have the exclusive privilege to put down stone crossings was rejected.

CAPTAIN JACK GETS LEFT.

The petition of John Walsh for an allowance of $15 for the use of a wagon to bring the remains of Nelms to the stationhouse, and also the use of one to go ten miles in the country to investigate the cause of death of Williams, was very properly rejected. It is understood that Chief Davis offered to pay the undertaker for the use of the wagon in the Nelms case. The petitioner, for some cause or other, does not fail to mention that the men, Nelms and Williams, were killed by police officers.

The petition for a cedar-block pavement on Monroe, from Desoto to Front street, was received and filed.

RESOLUTIONS.

Major Burke offered a resolution that the office of sewer and city engineer be consolidated and that the engineer in charge be authorized to employ an assistant at a salary of not exceeding $125 per month. Adopted.

A resolution was offered by Mr. Wallace to order a sidewalk on Lauderdale street. Adopted.

Mr. Lee offered a resolution that the property owners on the north side of Winchester street, between Center alley and Front or Chickasaw street, be required to lay or put down a brick sidewalk within thirty days.

Mr. Lee also offered the following resolutions, which were adopted:

Resolved, That the owners of property on the north side of Adams street, and east of the bayon, be required to pave the sidewalk with brick within thirty days.

Resolved, That the owners of property on the southeast corner of Adams and Third street be required to lay a brick sidewalk on Third street within thirty days.

APPOINTMENTS.

Messrs. Graves, James and Kney were appointed hospital trustees.

Messrs. Burke, James and Lee were appointed the Sewer Committee.

The bridge matter on Lauderdale street, first bayon south of Vance, was referred to the engineer.

A petition to pave Union street from De Soto to Brinkley avenue was received and filed.

ELECTION OF INSPECTOR.

On motion, the council proceeded to elect an inspector of weights and measures. This was somewhat exciting and required seven ballots to decide. There were twelve names before the council, Messrs. Dukes, Hall, Barinds, Harris, Mallory, Smith, Holmes, Merrill, McGuire, Ball, Conn and DeGroat. The voting was as follows:

First ballot—Dukes 1, Mallory 2, Holmes 1, Conn 1, DeGroat 1.

Second ballot—Dukes 2, Mallory 2, Conn 1, DeGroat 2.

Third ballot—Dukes 2, Mallory 1, Smith 1, DeGroat 3.

Fourth ballot—Dukes 1, Barinds 1, Mallory 1, DeGroat 3.

Fifth ballot—Dukes 3, Barinds 1, Mallory 2, DeGroat 1.

Sixth ballot—Dukes 2, Conn 2, DeGroat 3.

Seventh ballot—Dukes 2, Conn 1, DeGroat 4.

Mr. DeGroat was declared elected.

The council then adjourned.
