Augusta Chronicle of Friday.

Yesterday afternoon a report reached this city from Hamburg that a terrible crime had just been committed in that village. A Chronicle representative immediately hurried to the spot and obtained the following particulars:

About four o'clock Mr. George W. Damm, generally known as Willie Damm, commenced to get ready to come over to the city with his wife, for the purpose of visiting some relatives, it being her birthday. He was standing in a hall in his residence talking to his wife and sister, when a negro named Harry Hackett, employed by Mr. Roll, Mr. Damm's brother-in-law, walked up and stood close by, listening to the conversation. Mr. Damm remarked to Hackett that he had no business there and ordered him away. As he showed some reluctance to leave, Mr. Damm kicked at him, whereupon the negro put his hand behind him as if to draw a pistol, and retreated into Mr. Roll's store adjoining. Mr. Damm, who had no weapon, followed him, but when he reached a room next to the store he was caught hold of by his wife and sister. While they were standing thus Hackett, who was behind the counter in the store, fired at Mr. Damm. The ball missed the latter, but struck Mrs. Damm over the left eye, burying itself in the brain. She immediately sank to the ground, Mrs. Roll exclaiming, "My God! she is dead!" Mr. Damm pursued Hackett, who had now gone into the street. As Mr. Damm approached, Hackett fired a second shot, but the ball flew wide of the mark. A third followed, the missile striking Mr. Damm in the right shoulder, inflicting a slight flesh wound. Mr. Damm now threw a razor hone which he had in his pocket at Hackett, striking him on the head. At the same time he rushed at the assassin and grasped his hand, but the negro, a powerful fellow, jerked loose and fired a fourth shot. The ball missed its mark, but the discharge of the pistol was so close to Mr. Damm that the powder burned his chin. Hackett then escaped. A search was organized and threats were freely made that if he was caught the law would not be called upon to punish him.
When the Chronicle reporter saw Mrs. Damm she appeared to be in a dying condition, and it was not thought that she would live through the night. She had only been married a year.

A TRAGEDY IN HAMBURG.—On Thursday afternoon at 4 o'clock, while William Damm, a young man living in Hamburg, was talking to his wife and sister in his store, a negro named Harry Hackett came up and stood listening to the conversation. Damm ordered him away, whereupon the negro put his hand behind him as if to draw a pistol. Damm went towards him, but was held by his wife and sister. Hackett then fired at Damm, but missed him and struck his wife in the head, inflicting a fatal wound. Damm pursued Hackett who fired three times more at him, one of the balls striking him in the shoulder, causing a flesh wound. Another was fired so close that the powder burned Damm's face. Hackett escaped. Search is being made for him. There is much excite-caught he will be lynched.

—A special to the News and Courier, dated January 10, from Beaufort, gives the particulars of a fatal shooting, which took place at Bull river to-day, resulting in the death of one man and the serious wounding of two others. William J. Sweeny, keeper of a sailors' boarding house in Charleston, undertook to furnish four sailors to the British barkentine Sunbeam, lying at Bull river, and delivered the sailors on board that morning. As Sweeney was shoving off from the ship three of the sailors jumped back into his boat, when the captain of the vessel opened fire on them, killing one of the sailors and seriously wounding Sweeney and another sailor. The sheriff has gone to Bull river to arrest the captain.

Homicide in Hamburg.
At Hamburg, in this State, on the 13th inst., a negro named Harry Hackett, got into an altercation with a Mr. Damm, drew his pistol, fired at him, but missed his aim, and killed his wife. The negro fired three times more at Damm, one of the balls striking him in the shoulder, inflicting a flesh wound. Hackett escaped into Augusta, but a party pursued and if he is caught Judge Lynch will doubtless have a case.

See notice of Mr. Gray. He will certainly rent the Magnolia Hotel to the party who gives the most for it. Be in time and don't lose a bargain.

The obituary of Mrs. W. H. Curry in another column tells the sad tale of her death. We sympathize with the bereaved husband and grief stricken relatives.

'Who'll Go Back to Georgia'

The Grand Cotton Exposition opens at Atlanta, Ga., Oct. 5th, and closes December 31st, 1881. Many of our citizens desire to be in attendance, but we wish to know who will go back to Georgia to the Great Exposition?

Our friends are daily falling by the wayside—resting from all their toils. They should be placed in the best coffins that can be secured. The coffin is the home of the dead, and their only abiding place. Therefore, without solicitation, we say, go to Joe G. Kelso's and get a good coffin, a good home, for your dead relative or friend.

We are sorry to record the fact that Rev. L. W. Baker was seriously hurt Monday morning about 9 o'clock. Uncle Berry had preached at Dorcheat church on Sunday, and was on his way to Mars Hill, in company with Major Poe and sons when a dog ran up behind and frightened his mule, causing it to dash the buggy against a fence, tearing it to pieces, and throwing Rev. Baker to the ground.

have seen this year.

The rain has come, a little of it, and more is coming. Now move things lively, as suggested in other articles.

Mr. W. W. Souter is building a twelve or fourteen hundred dollar residence. This is the way to make home happy and build up a country.

"LYING OUT."—Saturday night Sunday light and Monday night—Baily.

"LYING IN."—Three colored stalwarts—County jail.

Our young friend, Charlie Goode, is going to housekeeping, and wishes to trade his hound pup for feathers. Don't all speak at once, though it is a goode bargain.

Capt Dixon returned from Little Rock Tuesday evening, chock full of railroad news. Hurrah tor Magnolia; perhaps we will get a depot here. Who knows?

Elsewhere we publish a list of the Grand and Petit Jurors for the fall term of court, as furnished by the commissioners. They will confer a special favor by calling on the Sheriff when they come to town, saving mileage in summoning them.

Lemons, formerly of this county, shot and killed Mr. Henry Cox near Dikes Ferry, La., last week. It was one of the coldest blooded murders of which we have ever heard. He waylaid Cox and shot him four times. So says the dead man's son.

We acknowledge a pleasant call Tuesday from Mrs. Jane Gray, who has just returned from a lengthy country visit, and Miss Sallie Drew, who is good enough looking and pleasant enough to make even an old batchelor feel happy, leaving editor's and young men out of the calculation. Call again, ladies.

Mr. C. P. Thornton informs us that a negro women named Campbell killed two of her own children with a pine knot, on Frank Hall place, near Dykes mills, La., last week. An inquest was held by Esq. Sikes; Dr. Day examined the dead children. We learn that the citizens, both white and black, gathered, tied the heartless murderess to a stake and burned her. Shocking, shocking to every sense of humanity both deeds.

The Bibles and Testaments of the American Bible Society for the Magnolia Auxiliary Society have been received and are now on deposit at A. J. Brewer's. Call and examine them. Testaments, from a nickel up. Bibles from 25 cents to 3 50.

HANSON & SPRIGGS.
Shot and in Jail.

Last week Esq. Baily, of Boon township, issued a writ of arrest against Hawthorne, (col.) for stealing corn. Constable Locket and Geo Starnes went to make the arrest but Hawthorne fled. Starnes, Montgomerv, Smith and two negroes were then deputised to make the arrest; the rogue fled the second time, and when Starnes fired his gun in the air to scare him, thinking he would then stop, instead of doing so he turned and fired three shots at one of the colored men; whereupon Starnes, Smith and the other colored man all fired at him, lodging buck and squirrel shot enough in his body to bring him to the ground. He is now in jail, awaiting the action of the Grand Jury.

Crops being so very short will enable the farmer to get through with the gathering soon, and all will have ample time to sow small grain before the wintry blasts set in. Now don't neglect this important crop. Wheat, rye, barley, oats and millet; in fact, anything and everything that will do for food for man or beast should be sown. We know one man cannot be expected to sow all kinds of grain, but every man can sow one kind to great advantage. Fall first, then spring oats should be liberally sown by every farmer. We

also recommend that the best land be used for this purpose. Where cotton has been raised this year land is in the best condition for sowing.

COLONEL POTTER'S FATE.
COLONEL POTTER'S FATE.
Tareco of His Murderers Now in Jail a
Albuquerque.
The worst abominations concerning
The worst apprehensions concerning Colonel Charles Potter, step-son of ex-Governor Van Zandt, of Newport, R. I., are justified by the dispatches received on Monday from St. Louis to the effect that New Mexican detectives had ascertained that the missing man was murdered and robbed by three Mexicans.

Colonel Potter was a member of one of the most distinguished families of Rhode Island, and he leaves an estimable wife, three lovely children and an elegant home in Newport. He was very fond of yachting and other out-door sports, and seemed to be at home wherever there was a prospect of danger. He went West last summer, and while not being obliged to work, he accepted a position under Colonel Emmons, he accepted a position under Colonel Emmons, of the United States geological survey. When in the mining regions he wrote a number of very interesting letters for the Providence Journal. The last letter received by his wife was dated October 14. In this letter he stated that he would leave for home in a short time. His grief-stricken parents have left nothing undone that would tend to ferret out his whereabouts and to solve the painful mystery. While they had grave apprehensions for his safety, they never were willing to believe that he was dead.

Colonel Potter, who was about thirty years of age, studied at Brown university. He was a member of Governor Van Zandt's personal staff during his three terms as governor. He was a young man of more than ordinary ability, and was respected by all friends acquaintances.

The Murderers Lynched.

A despatch to the News from Albuquerque, N. M., of the 31st ult., says: "A few days since Sheriff Arligo effected the arrest of Escalero Pera at Isletta, N. M., on the charge of having murdered Col. Chas. Potter, of the United States geological survey, who left Alburquerque on Oct. 14, last, for the new placer mining camp, since which time he has not been heard of. Pera confesses having been a witness of the crime, although not a participant, and says Colonel Potter was waylaid in a canon near San Antonio, and, after a desperate resistance, was killed, the body robbed and buried. Sheriff Arligo, accompanied by Pera, went to search the spot, and returning this evening brought the body of the murdered man. He also captured Lieuel Barrea and a Mexican known as California Joe, who were accessories. Dallnant Pantaleon Siera, another, was hanged by the Vigilantes at Barnalillo recently for horse stealing. Pera, Barrea and California Joe were taken from the jail last night by a band of masked men and hanged on the porch of the building. Not a word was spoken, and it was scarcely fifteen minutes from the time the band approached the jail until the three men were disposed of. Sheriff Arligo is on the track of Leiber, the principal in the crime, and expects to effect his capture to-day. Col. Potter had been collecting statistics for the census bureau.

LITTLE ROCK. Three Negro Murderers Lynched—Asylum Building Contract Awarded. Special to the Appeal.] LITTLE ROCK, June 8.—The contract for the construction of the State lunatic asylum was to-night awarded to Thalman & Clark, of this city, the bid being $460 less than Piper, of Memphis. The contract price is $144,440. News reached the city to-night that R. F Hall, a prominent farmer of Sevier county, was murdered by three negroes he had employed to ferry him across Rolling Fork creek. The whites organized and captured the negroes and hung them to a tree on the bank of the creek at the scene of the crime. To be Tried for Manslaughter.
To be Tried for Manslaughter.

CEDAR RAPIDS, IA., June 8.—The coroner's jury, after a thorough investigation as to the cause of the railroad disaster on Sunday morning last, on the Cedar Rapids and Northern railroad, four miles west of this city, whereby Frank Horton and Thomas Hurley were killed, returned a verdict this afternoon, finding the death of these two men was caused by cuttable and criminal negligence of Charles B. Lewis, night operator at Cedar Rapids. Lewis was taken into custody. Information has been filed before Justice Anderson by W. F. Fitch, General Claim agent of the above-named road, charging Lewis with the crime of manslaughter. He will have a preliminary examination tomorrow.

That Mexican Colonization Scheme.

TOPEKA, KS., June 8.—The Mexican Colonization company co-operative have named the President of the United States and the President of Mexico as ex-officio members of the Board of Directors, with power to appoint proxies. It proposes to engage in settling the Northern States of Mexico with cooperative colonies on a grand scale. More than 4000 colonists have been enrolled. The lowest rates of fare will be obtained for companies of colonists from their homes to the company's lands, and they will be moved in large numbers systematically. Agents will be employed in every county in America. The headquarters are at Topeka, Kansas.

Jay Gould Reaching Northward.

Jay Gould Reaching Northward.

OMAHA, June 8.—Articles of incorporation were filed here to-day for the Missouri Pacific Railway company in Nebraska. The principal place for the transaction of business is Omaha. The incorporators are Jay Gould, A. A. Talmage, F. B. 1rake, S. M. Smith and J. T. Webster. It is understood they will build a riverwise line from Omaha to connect with the Missouri Pacific at Atchison or St. Joe.

A Fatal Arkansas Cutting.

LITTLE ROCK, June 8.—The Gazette's Fort Smith special says: "A difficulty occurred yesterday at Oak Bower, a small village near this place, between Pres Ingraham and Andy Rhea, about a well-auger, in the course of which Ingraham cut Rhea in the bowels, inflieting fatal cuts. Ingraham took to the woods and escaped."

A BREAK FOR FREEDOM. Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune. Augusta, Me., June 8.—There was a good deal of excitement at Thomaston to-day over the desperate attempt of two convicts to escape from the State Prison, and fears were entertained of a general attempt to break jail. During the day Haynes, the Rockland murderer, and a Portland thief named Bragdon, on their way to the shops threw some lintment and pepper into the eyes of the guard, completely blinding him. They then rushed across the guard-room and rushed at the outer guard with a bowle-knife and the pepper, but the guard raised his rifle and fired, the ball passing through Haynes' right lung. Bragdon ran back in time to escape the second shot from the rifle, and both men were secured and found to be fully armed. It is believed Haynes had made arrangements for a general jail delivery. He killed his guard at Rockland a few years ago, and this is his third or fourth attempt at escape, all of his plans involving the killing or maining of the guards or watchmen. SPEEDY JUSTICE.
LITTLE Rock, Ark., June 8.—The details of a murder and a triple lynching in Sevier County were received to-day. The murdered man was R. F. Hall, who lived in the vicinity of Locksburg, and who had started for an adjacent county for the purpose of visiting friends. Upon reaching Rolling Fork Creek he found the waters very high and dangerous, and hired three negroes to assist him across. The darkeys, believing he had a large sum of money, assaulted him, knocking him down after a sharp scuffle, and rilling his pockets. The thieves secured twenty-five or thirty cents, and enraged at the smallness of the sum, or fearing the consequences, they completed their work by strangling the old man and throwing the body into the water. It floated down the stream some distance and lodged in the branches of a fallen tree. By some means a clew to the murderers became public. A band of armed men set out to hunt them down. The ringleader was captured first. He confessed, and begged piteously for life, but was taken back to the banks of the creek and hung to the limb of a tree. Tuesday, at nightfall, the two remaining murderers were captured, and, by midnight, were brought back to the scene of their crime. Ropes were procured, and presently the guilty wretches were dangling from the limb of an adjacent tree. The crime and punishment have created a whirlwind of excitement in the immediate vicinity of the scene, though the action of Judge Lynch is universally approved.

Horrible Tragedy in Arkansas.
Lynne Boog, Ark, June 10.—The
Horrible Tragedy in Arkansas.
LITTLE BOOK, Ark., June 10.—The particulars of a horrible tragedy near Looksburg, in Levier county, have been received. B. F. Hall, a wealthy farmer, started to visit friends in an adjoining county. He was eccentric and, it was generally reported, carried a large sum of money. Beaching Rolling Fork creek, he found it swollen by recent rains. He hired three negroes to assist him across. While apparently making arrangements they suddenly sprang on the unfortunate man and felled him to the earth. In rifting the victim's pockets the assessors found but thirty cents. Enraged at not finding more, they seized him by the throat and choked him to death, and tied stones to the body to keep it down, as they supposed, sufficiently to carry it to the bottom of the stream, but it lodged in some drift below, where it was seen and recognized by a colored man. Next day the news was spread. A large body of white men soon gathered where the trace of the murderers was struck. After a few hours' pursuit one of the gang was caught and brought back to the ford and strung up to a tree. Search was resumed and about dark his two companions were found in the woods. They confessed all and were taken back to the ford and hung beside their companion.

James Chesley, a resident of Lee, New Hampshire, was stabbed to death in a quarrel with an old acquaintance, in Newmarket, Minnesota, a few days ago.
Thomas Boyer, aged 17 years, shot and killed an unknown man without any apparent provocation, at Vincennes, Indiana, on Wednesday last.

Incensed, it is, supposed, at not fluding more, they soiled Hall by the throat and choked him till life was extinct, then tled stones to the corpse, weighing it down, as they supposed, sufficiently to carry it to the bottom of the stream, but it lodged in a drift below, where it was seen and recognized by a colored man next day. BETWEEN $90,000 and $100,000 in
bonds, from which coupons had just been cut, were stolen from the Treasurer's desk of the Erie County Savings Bank at Buffalo, N. Y. A number of the bonds have been traced to Baltimore.

WILLIAM MURPHY, the divorced husband of Mrs. Newton McClarren, visited that lady at her residence near Pittsburgh, Pa., the other day, and requested an interview. When she appeared, Murphy threw his arms around her neck, and, while thus embracing her, shot her in the back and breast, and then placing the revolver against his forehead, fired a bullet through his brain, killing himself instantly. Mrs. McClarren, it is thought, will recover.

JAMES MALONE, Patrick Hunter and Gerald Sanders, employed in the Andes Mine, Virginia City, Nev., were suffocated by gas the other day. Several miners were made ill in endeavoring to recover the bodies.

LEADING manufacturers of agricultural implements in the West are said to have greatly curtailed operations on account of unfavorable advices regarding the coming harvest.

LEWIS SWEDEN, an old farmer, of Van Buren County, Ark., was assassinated on the porch of his dwelling, recently, by three men who sprang from the shrubbery and riddled his body with bullets. Supposed to be the work of moonshiners.

MUNLEY ELLIS and Wright Newsome, two young men living near Wilson, N. C., met in a field and began quarreling on the 7th. Ellis had a pistol, and finally drew it and shot Newsome in the head, killing him instantly. The two gentlemen had some time ago been paying attention to the same young lady, and this was the beginning of bad feeling between them.

A NEW ALBANY & Chicago Railroad conductor named Davis undertook to climb on top of a car near Pekin, Ind., and was knocked off by the timbers of the bridge across Blue River, and instantly killed. His body fell into the river, and was recovered by the train-men and taken to New Albany. He had only been on the road a few days.

At the village of Chesaning, Mich., recently, a party of roughs connected with a circus, armed with clubs, proceeded to break up a dance. Augustus Emery, a policeman, was pounded to death; Fred Wenzer was fatally injured; J. B. Griswold, village President, was severely wounded; Charles Hamer received a pistol ball in the side of the face and a dozen others were cut and bruised. Thirteen of the gang were arrested, and with difficulty the people were restrained from lynching them.

The National Millers' Association held their eighth annual Convention at Chicago, beginning on the 7th. The Cochran patent cases, representing claims for damages to the amount of $36,000,000 against members of the Association, were settled by compromise, the terms of which are private.

The completion of the Fayetteville (Ark.) Branch of the St. Louis & San Francisco Railroad was celebrated on the 8th, at Fayetteville, with great ceremony.

The Theater Royal, Belfast, Ireland, was entirely destroyed by fire on the 8th.

The negroes who murdered a farmer named A. F. Hall, near Lockesburg, Sevier County, Ark., were hanged by an infuriated party of citizens.

During a severe storm near Wheeling, West Va., on the 8th, a family named Straub, living on Glenn's Run, were swept away in the night, the mother and five children being drowned and the father carried on a log to the head of one of the Sisters' Islands, where he was found in an insensible condition.

An explosion on the steamer John H. Hannah, near New Orleans, on the 8th, resulted in serious injury to eleven colored deckhands. Some of the victims were literally flayed alive.
hull-murder-suspects-three-unnamed-negro.A23: Three negroes of Looksburg, Ark., were mistaken in supposing that a traveler whom they ferried across the river carried a large amount of money, for after murdering him they found only $1 in his pockets. But nobody lived within several miles, and they felt no fear of detection after throwing the weighted remains into the stream. That was a second mistake, for a freshet occurred suddenly, and the remains were washed ashore by the force of the current. A third mistake was in believing that no great effort would be made to capture them, their victim having no friends in that region. A party of mounted lynchers pursued them three days, and hanged them without trial.

The Railroad War.

NEW YORK, July 25th.—The railroad ticket war continues. All the trunk lines are now selling tickets to Chicago at $9.

The New York Collectorship.

NEW YORK, July 25th.—Judge Robertson this afternoon took the oath of office as Collector of the Port.

Comet "C" Seen at Washington.

WASHINGTON, July 25th.—A new comet, or comet "C," was seen at the Naval Observatory here yesterday morning, and again this morning. Professor Eastman, of the Naval Observatory, said to day: "I saw it last night, or rather this morning. I had only five minutes in which to observe it, no account of the clouds, and of course did not see very much. I expect it will be visible to the naked eye in about ten days. It will not go so far north as the other. We will be able to see it early in the evening in the west and early in the morning in the east. It has something of a tail, which will grow more distinct. The comet is labeled as comet 'C,' being the third discovered this year. The comet up by the pole star is comet 'B.'"

A Fiendish Act Promptly Punished.

MEMPHIS, July 25th.—The Avalanche's Yazoo City (Miss.) special says: A rape was committed last Saturday on a young lady by a negro named Isaac Fisher. He threw her in a cistern to drown her, but the water being too shallow he slid down the chain and held her head under water until she drowned. He then tried to climb the chain, but found himself caged and was soon detected. The demon was summarily dealt with, and in all probability is now taking a chat with Tobey Wells, who was hanged here last Thursday.

The Missouri Train Robbers.

ST. LOUIS, July 25th.—The Governor will offer the largest reward the law allows for the capture of the train robbers. He censures the citizens and authorities of the county in which the robbery occurred for not being diligent in the detection and arrest of
the capture of the train robbers. The captures the citizens and authorities of the county in which the robbery occurred for not being diligent in the detection and arrest of these men. A consultation between the Governor and the railroad authorities will be held to-morrow.

The Lumbermen's Strike.

EAU CLAIRE (Wis.), July 25th.—The strike has apparently ended, but many of the strikers have left, and the owners of the mills can hardly supply their places.

An Easy Victory.

LEADVILLE (Col.), July 25th.—The tenile race between Miss Minnie Pinneau, of Greeley, Col., and Miss Curtis, of Topeka, Ks., resulted in an easy victory for the former. On the eighth mile Pinneau was one mile and a half ahead, when Curtis dismounted and fainted on the track. Pinneau finished the race in twenty-six minutes.

Body Found.

DENVER (Col.), July 25th.—A Santa Fe special says: The body of a man named Von Weg, of Waterbury, Conn., has been found by the Pueblo Indians in the Rio Grande river. The body contained two bullet holes, and it is supposed that Von Weg was murdered by two companions with whom he was travelling.

A New Bishop.

CHICAGO, July 25th.—Bishop McMullen was consecrated here to-day as Archbishop of the newly created diocese of Davenport, Iowa. There was a large attendance of Catholic clergy.

A Case Where the Minority Should Have Ruled?
NEW ORLEANS, July 26 — A special dispatch from Yazoo City to the Democrat says, information was received there yesterday of a horrible affair which occurred near Satartia, in which a white girl was outraged and murdered by a colored blacksmith, named Issac Fisher. The latter, thinking he had killed the girl by choking her, threw her body into a well, and then went to the shop, near by. Returning after a little while, he found the girl standing in the water, which was two and a half feet deep; whereupon, going down upon the rope, he drowned her, but was then unable to get out, and was found there with the dead body of his victim. The citizens who had assembled took a vote on the question of hanging him, but some circumstances in the case caused the majority to favor holding him unil an inquest had been held.
isaac-fisher-satartia-1881-07-25.A6:
An Outrage in Yazoo.
AZOO CITY. Miss. July 25.
YAZOO CITY, Miss., July 25.—On Saturday last, near Satartia, in the county, a negro named Isaac Fisher committed at outrage upon the person of a young white lady who was alone at home, and after the outrage choked her and threw her down a cistern. Returning shortly and seeing her standing up in the water which was not more than two feet deep, the fiend descended the rope and drowned her, but could not get up the rope and bung caught in the cistern said the lady fell in and he went down to rescue her but too late. Upon examination by physicians it was seen that the victim had been ravished, and the negro, who had been freed, was re arrested, and the crowd agreed to hang him, but a majority present decided to hold him till after the Coroner's inquest, and he was to be hanged to-day, and doubtless ere this the wretch has met a deserved death at the hands of Judge Lynch.—Vicksburg Herald.

On Monday the wretch was hung in the presence of two or three hundred people.
isaac-fisher-satartia-1881-07-25.A11:
Consistency.
The Memphis Avalanche of the 28th. contains a carefully prepared article beginning with these words: "Lynch law is anarchy. The rule of the mob is the nullification of the law. The Avalanche is opposed to a state of anarchy, because it is a condition destructive of all the interests which men can have in a country, &c.," and winds it up with, "It is a crime, which the Avalanche will not cease to denounce."

This is all right and in keeping with the teachings of a great and popular newspaper; but the fat of that article as it were, is knocked into the fire, by the very next one below it in the same column. It is introduced with a six inch double leaded heading, surmounted with a two-line pica sensational catch line which reads, "Retribution." Then follows a pen picture, in approved style, with sickening details, of the violation of the person of a young lady by a brutal negro, who threw his victim in a cistern. The water being too shallow to drown her, the negro slipped down the chain, and chucked her head under until she was drowned. He then then endeavored to climb up the chain to the mouth of the cistern, but this teat he was unable to perform, and was, so to speak, caught in his own trap. Here he was discovered and the neighbors gathered; he was drawn up, and with a rope and a convenient limb, short work was made with the limb, short work was made with the rapist. All this this is described in language and expression indicating that the the Avalanche believes that circumstances alters cases, and that heroic treatment is sometimes necessary to the suppression of crime, as well as in the treatment of bad cases of disease.
isaac-fisher-satartia-1881-07-25.A12:
A Horrid Deed Committed by a Negro.
YAZOO CITY, July 25. — Last Saturday a negro man named Isaac Fisher came upon a respectable young lady who happened to be alone at a house. He assaulted her and succeeded in violating her person. He then threw her into a cistern. The water was too shallow to drown her. The man Fisher then slipped down the chain used for drawing water from the cistern. When he had descended to the bottom he caught the poor girl whom he had so cruelly used, and chucked her head down until she was drowned. THE MURDERER HUNG.

On Saturday morning at about 8 o'clock, Rosa Ertel, a German girl, who was living with Mr. F. W. Dalton about ten miles below Satartia, refusing to accede to the demands of Isaac Fisher, was seized by him and dragged into his house and forced to submit to his hellish desigus. But the demon did not stop here. The poor, delicate and consumptive girl announced her intention to inform Mr. Dalton, when the fiend pressed her to the floor and a desperate struggle ensued in which she actually tore into threads the shirt, vest and pants which Fisher wore, and he bruised and beat her arms, breast and face as black as midnight, constantly pressing all the time his right hand upon her throat until her body was, as he thought, entirely lifeless. Nor did he stay his murderous hand here, for had he done so poor Rosa Ertel would not now be wrapped in the habiliments of the grave. His evil genius immediately invented a way to hide forever from the world his crime and he dragged the lifeless girl to a cistern about fifteen feet distant, which was only used for washing purposes, and dropped her in. His heart no doubt felt lighter as he turned away and thought his crime forever obscured, but he was destined to disappointment. He went back shortly to see if the body had sung and to his dismay the girl was standing up and bracing her hand against the cistern wall, having been revived by the influence of the cold water. "Still the villain pursued her," and quickly lowering himself into the cistern by sliding down the chain dependent from the windlass above, he again seized the girl, already more dead than alive and pressing her beneath the water stood upon her frail body until life was extinct by strangulation.

The demon's hour had, however at last come. His attempt to ascend the small trace chain out of the cistern proved to be futile, and the libertine and victim was caged with the body of his outraged and dead victim. He said he went into the cistern to save the girl whom he say fall in,
and after getting down was compelled to
stand upon her body to prevent himself from
drowning, not withstanding the fact that
the water was scarcely two and a half feet
deep. Fisher was in the cistern an hour
and thirty minutes, and finding no means of
escape, he was forced to call for help. The
facts as above stated are taken from his con-
fession. The girl's body was taken out, but
Messrs. Dalton and Brown both being absent
from home until Saturday night, no arrest
were made until Sunday, when Esquire A.
H. Montgomery empanneled a jury and had
an examination before them by Dr. J. B.
Taylor, which elicited the main facts.
Fisher was brought to Satartia Sunday
evening and a meeting of citizens decided
he was guilty, but deferred further action
till yesterday, (Monday) morning. Early
in the morning a crowd began to gather in
town. Stern, resolute men in groups gave
no uncertain indications of the sequel to
follow. At half past nine o'clock there was
seen moving down the street a column two
or three strong, and halting in front of the
house in which Fisher was guarded, they
overpowered the guards and soon emerged
with the prisoner and placed him in front.
The work done afterward required only a
few minutes. Visitors to the town in a half
hour passed the tell-tale spectacles of a man's
body suspended by a rope from the limb of
a peacan tree, not more than ten feet from
the roadside. It was the body of Isaac
Fisher, the libertine and murderer.

SATARTIA, MISS., July 25.
Our little village and the surround.

SATARTIA, Miss., July 25.

Our little village and the surrounding community was thrown into intense exaltement Sunday morning last upon hearing of a most brutal outrage committed upon the person of a young white girl, named Rosa Eatle, residing six miles from here, on the plantation known as Brown and Dalton, the deed being done by a negro man, named Isiah Fisher, working on the same place as a blacksmith.

On the morning of July 23rd the negro named above, watching his opportunity, seized the girl, and dragging her into his house, and there outraged her in the most brutal manner. After knocking her senseless, he dragged her to the cistern, only a short distance from the house, and after throwing her in, went back to his work. Not feeling satisfied that she was dead, he went to the cistern the second time, and finding her still alive, went down in the cistern, holding to the chain, there to finish his hellish work, choking and beating her, and then standing on her, body until the flendish work was complete, he being in the cistern at least an hour and a half. Finding he could not ascend the chain, he began calling for assistance, claiming he went there to save the young girl's life.

An inquest was held over the body of the dead girl Sunday morning, and the physician attending pronounced it, after careful examination, to be one of the most brutal outrages ever committed upon a female. The negro (Isiah Fisher) was arrested and brought to town Sunday night. The white and colored citizens held a meeting that night, some agreeing and others disagreeing as regards to the manner of his punishment. On Monday morning, Fisher having confessed he was guilty of the crime, about ten o'clock, the surrounding country, both black and white, with out further delay, swung him to the nearest tree, just outside of our village, where he remained hanging until two o'clock the same day. The body was then lowered, and the verdict of the coroner's jury was that said Fisher came to his death by hanging. There was about three hundred persons present.

From the Durango RECORD.
This morning about 2

This morning, about 3 o'clock, Mabel Young and Fat Alice had a quarrel in the Coliseum auditorium, and in a short time were pulling each other's hair. Tom Lynch and Jack Roberts were present and took part in the affray, either with the intent of separating the parties or for the purpose of aiding one of them. Mr. Greatorex, who had attended the entertainment and lingered behind a few moments after it closed, seeing, as he supposed, a woman in distress, instinctively interfered for the purpose of assisting her out of it, but had no sooner done so than he was struck on the head by Jack Roberts, with a revolver. The blow knocked Greatorex down, and stunned him considerably; and before he could arise Roberts drew his revolver and deliberately shot him in the back, the ball entering near the base of the spine and passing through the sacrum in a downward direction on the left side. Marshal Heathy, in his efforts to stop the disturbance, was also struck on the head with a revolver, by whom he does not know, and severely injured. Roberts escaped during the excitement, through a side door, into a hallway which leads to the rear of the Coliseum building, and he has not been seen since. Mr. Greatorex was laid on a table in the auditorium, bleeding profusely, and Drs. Plumb and Clay were called, who at once removed him to the office of the San Juan Lumber Co., on Railroad street, where they have faithfully attended him ever since. They have but little hope for his recov-
jack-roberts-durango-1881-03-25.A2: ery, although it is barely possible that he may live. The wound is not necessarily fatal of itself, but the shock to his nervous system was very great, the muzzle of the revolver being so close to his person when fired that his clothes were burned. Everything possible is being done for him and we can only hope for the best. A reward of $500 is offered by the leading citizens of Durango, for the capture of Roberts, dead or alive,and the chances are that Roberts will be captured.

A COLORADO TRAGEDY.
The Murder of Mr. Thomas A. Greatorex,
a Former Resident of Washington.
Many now here will remember the bright, dashing lad, Thomas A. Greatorex, who, about 1864, entered the service of the Government as a messenger in the Note Division Office of the Secretary of the Treasury, and who, a few days after his appointment, having obtained permission to see United States notes destroyed, discovered the witness for the Treasurer, — Cornwell, slip some half notes in his coat pocket instead of throwing them in the furnace, and reporting this to the chief of the division, was brought before General Spinner, where he stoutly affirmed the truth of what he had seen. Means were at once taken to detect Cornwell, and the result was a confession and trial and the return of some thirty thousand dollars to the Treasury. Young Greatorex was afterward promoted to a clerkship. He was born in New York, and was the son of the celebrated organist, H. W. Greatorex, and Eliza Greatorex, the artist. His father died in Charleston, S. C., while he was a child. His mother and sisters are now in Algiers. As near as the facts can now be ascertained, young Greatorex had gone from his home in Silverton, Col., to Durango, and while there, in protecting a woman from the assaults of a rufian, was knocked down and shot on the 6th instant; he died on the 16th. He was greatly beloved, and had a host of friends in the State he had chosen for a permanent home. The citizens of Silverton offered a reward of $500 for the capture of the murderer, and a telegram in Sunday's papers tells that he had been caught and lynched.
jack-roberts-durango-1881-03-25.A14: knocked her down. WASHINGTON, March 31.—Senator Conkling has determined to wage war against Robertson and the administration. He holds Secretary Blaine responsible for the nomination. The Indian Bureau has been advised by Agent Tiffany, under date of San Carlos, Arizona, October 2d, that on Saturday, "issue pay," troops went from Camp Thomas to the sub-agency to arrest Chiefs George and Bonito. The Director of the Mints has authorized the Superintendent of the Philadelphia Mint to strike memorial medals bearing the heads of Presidents Lincoln and Garfield on opposite sides. The large gold medals will be sold for $9, small sized for $4.50; large sized silver medals for 60 cents, small sized for 25 cents. Similar medals containing the head of President Garfield on one side and a wreath on the other have been authorized, and will be sold at the same prices.

Last Friday Jacob Whitmore and his wife, "both very young and recently married," went into the woods near the house, at Huntsville, Ohio, to gather hickory nuts. Bishop O'Hara, in the cathedral at Scranton, and several priests, in the churches of the suburbs of that city, yesterday denounced from the altar the doings of the so-called "grave yard sharks." A case was instanced where a man was heavily insured after death and the assessments were collected.

Matthew W. Aylwin, one of the oldest pay clerks in the navy, died in Brooklyn on Saturday, aged 79 years. He was born in England, but came to America when a boy, and was employed in the navy for more than fifty years.

Ross has accepted the amended agreement for a race with Hanlan, and requests the latter to name the time and place. At the same time Ross signifies a preference for Washington on account of the lateness of the season.

President Arthur remained at his home in New York city yesterday and received few callers. Ex-Senator Conkling had not arrived in the city, and many doubted if he would attend the State Convention.

L. Ferry Young, a son of Brigham, died on board of the steamer Knickerbocker, from a Mexican port for New York, and was buried at sea, on the 28th ult. He was sick when he went on board.

FONTAINE O. Oct 1 — Oct 1
Wife Murder in Ohio.

BELLEFONTAINE, O., Oct. 1.—On the Lewis-town and Bellefontaine turnpike, eight miles from Bellefontaine, occurred yesterday afternoon one of the most horrible affairs that has ever blackened the history of this country. Jacob Whitmore, a farmer about 28 years of age, was married on the 17th of July to Orrie Short, 14 years of age, the daughter of a widow. Yesterday afternoon Whitmore took his girl-wife out into the woods to gather huckory nuts, accompanied by her little brother and sister. Whitmore soon returned, and was followed in a short time by his wife, who was suffering from horrible cramps accompanied by spasms. A physician was summoned, but she died about midnight in terrible agony. At first the poor girl denied that anything was wrong with her, but when she found that death could not be arrested, she confessed that her husband had compelled her to take a white powder, threatening to cut her throat if she refused. Whitmore is a country youth, and told the Times correspondent to night, when interviewed in jail, that his wife killed herself. His preliminary examination takes place on Monday, and if the evidence is strong against him he may be lynched, as occurred here a few years ago in the notorious Shell case, the people being terribly incensed.

At the inquest on Saturday it was testified that Whitmore bought strychnine two weeks ago; that he said a few days ago that his wife should not be alive in a week. The little brother of the girl-wife testified in his childish way, confirming his sister's statement that Jake made her swallow the poison "or he would cut her throat." A piece of paper was also found in the woods with strychnine adhering to it, where the villain had forced her to take it. The sheriff has carried the prisoner to an adjoining county to escape the mob which he had been notified would hang Whitmore tonight. The town is filling up rapidly with excited men and neighbors of the girl to assist in the hanging, but they have come on a fruitless errand.

SAYS a Mount Vernon correspondent: Great anxiety prevails among farmers relative to wheat planted in September. Heavy rains and warm weather have caused it to prematurely advance, and it is claimed that fully one-half the amount sown is rotating at the roots or being destroyed by the Hessian fly. The abundant clover crop promised has not panned out, and the granger wears an elongated face and azure countenance.

J. R. Muzem, of Barnesville, Belmont County, some days ago, started on his way to Milwaukee to wed an estimable young lady of that city. While en route he stopped at Chicago to see the sights. Drinking was of course a part of the programme, and it is stated that when Mr. Muzem wound up in the station-house on the verge of lunacy from excess of drink, it was found his spree had cost him $1,900. Mr. Muzem is well advanced in years, and well to do. He does not often drink, but when he does, everybody in his region is apt to find it out.

MRS. MARY FRY, the wife of a well-to-do farmer living north of Unionville, eloped with Jed Davis, a young man living with Fry as a farm hand. Davis left a note saying he was aware of the enormity of his offense, but Mary had mashed him, and he was powerless to resist the temptation. Mrs. Fry added a brief, business-like postscript, urging her husband to procure a decree of divorce right away and marry a certain widowed lady of the neighborhood, who, she was quite sure, would be good to the seven small Fry she was leaving to his care.

A STRANGER on horseback stopped at the farm-house of Fred Eaglehoff, five miles north of Plain City, and, after eating dinner and smoking with the farmer, made a proposition to trade horses, his being an excellent one, and soon after put his saddle on Eaglehoff's horse and rode it to try its speed, he said. Since Eaglehoff has seen neither stranger nor horse. On the evening of the same day a second party, claiming to come from Southern Ohio, called and laid claim to the stranger's horse as property stolen from him two nights before. Eaglehoff looked on the matter as a put-up job and refused to give up the animal.

ALL AROUND THE GLOBE.
The Servo-American treaty has been signed.
Michigan relief fund in New York, $107,-922.

The British troops are returning from Afghanistan.

The general convention of Universalists is in session at Detroit.

Senators Ingalls and Garland are preparing a national bankruptcy bill.

Owners at Copenhagen of the steamer Thingvallo think she is safe.

Preparations are making at Moscow for the coronation of Alexander III.

Electric lighting of cars on the London & Brighton railway is successful.

Secretary Windom has received $50 from Cleveland for the conscience fund.

Baron Haymerle's death postponed the czar's interview with Francis Joseph.

Ex-Gov. Fairchild, late minister to Spain, will not return to this country until spring.

Gen. Banks says he knows nothing of his alleged appointment as governor of Arizona.

Assim Pasha, minister of foreign affairs for Turkey, insists upon resigning his portfolio.

The fifth annual meeting of the American Humane association commenced yesterday in Boston.

Delegates to choose senators will be elected in France November 20. The final election is January 8.

A Fargo telegram says the rumor that King's balloon had been seen in that vicinity is unfounded.

Printer Defrees did not shut the printing office for the Yorktown holiday, and the employees complain.

The National carriage builders' association met at Cincinnati yesterday, President J. M. Bristow in the chair.

A Zanzibar dispatch says: The Belgian expedition under Rogers, with 135 natives, sails to-morrow to join Stanley on the Congs.

The fish commission steamer Fishhawk, has brought a large whale skeleton from Provincetown, Mass., for the national museum.

The ninth annual congress for the advancement of women opened yesterday at Buffalo. Delegates were present from all parts of the Union.

A North Walden, Vt., farmer writes Treasurer Gilfillan asking if $225 of notes which his cow chewed can be redeemed. They can if distinguishable.

The five experts appointed by the general association of underwriters of the United States to examine the fire department of St. Louis, have begun work.

About 10:30 yesterday morning J. B. Ames, a prominent miller of Sandusky, O., in trying to run a belt from a fly-wheel, was caught in the machinery and instantly killed.

The ninth annual meeting of Union prisoners occurred at Springfield, Ill., yesterday. It was attended by something over 200 prisoners of war, and many other veteran soldiers.

Owing to the discharge of a favorite foreman, 400 strippers in Lorillard's tobacco factory, Jersey City, are on a strike. This action of the girls causes the enforced idleness of 200 men.

The Albany, N. Y., Evening Journal says Judge Folger has had no authoritative information of the intention of the president to call him to assume the portfolio of the treasury department.

Harvey, owner of the Randolph mills, Philadelphia, found criminally responsible for loss of life in neglecting to furnish fire escapes, has been committed to await the action of the district attorney.

At Louisville, yesterday, a dog fight occurred between Pilot, of New York city, and Crib, of Louisville, for $1,000 a side. Pilot won after a battle of an hour, which ended in the death of the Louisville dog.

An order was entered and bond for $10,000 given in the United States circuit court at St. Louis yesterday, appointing John M. Douglas receiver of the Ohio & Mississippi railroad property within the jurisdiction of the court.

Randolph Disbrow, of the New Jersey battalion, had both hands blown off by the premature discharge of a cannon at Yorktown, yesterday. Both arms were amputated. The governor of New Jersey says Disbrow will be pensioned.

The annual session of the International brotherhood of locomotive engineers, assembled at Baltimore yesterday, with a full attendance of delegates from the United States and Canada. P. M. Arthur, grand chief engineer, of Cleveland, presided.

News has been received from Meca that two hostile factions there settled their differences by a battle outside the town, in which several were killed and wounded on both sides. Three battalions of troops and several batteries are ordered to Meca from Constantinople.

A stage between Alma and Fayetteville, Ark., met with a terrible accident. The horses running away, the stage collided with a stump. Wm. Sanders, the driver, was instantly killed, and of the three passengers, Mr. Brown, was fatally and G. C. Harris, and A. A. Threadgill, seriously hurt.

james-cunningham-helena-1881-10-19.A2:
Lynch Law in Arkansas.
CHICAGO, October 20.—A dispatch to the Daily News from Helena, Ark., says that three negroes charged with the murder of an overseer, named Magrath, were captured by a masked mob, and James Cunningham, one of them, was shot and left for dead. He turned up alive the next day denying his guilt and implicating white men in the murder. A posse is in pursuit of the mob.

CAN'T KILL HIM. An Arkansas Negro Who Has Been Twice Shot and Left for Dead Still Alive and Kicking. Rascalities of a Darky Doctor in Georgia-A Bold Bank Robbery Up in Illinois.
WACO, TEXAS., October 20.—Kit Hunston, who was stabbed at Hillsboro, by James Everett, is dead and Everett is in jail.

Murdered by Negroes.

McKINNEY, TEXAS, October 20.—Mr. Nowel, a well-to-do farmer, was murdered at his residence by a negro named Zach Lind-say and an unknown man. Cause—quarrel over a business transaction.

Died in the Line of His Duty.

PRESCOTT, ARIZ., October 20.—Deputy-Sheriff Briant was killed while in the discharge of his duty by a desperado named Miller. The murderer escaped. A large force is in search.

Went Through a Sleeper.

St. LOUIS, October 20.—George F. Roberts, an Englishman, was robbed of $1900 in a sleeping-car between Indianapolis and Litch-field, on the Indianappolis and St. Louis Road. Five other passengers were robbed of small sums.

Road Agents in Texas.

HENRIETTA, TEXAS, October 20.—The mail coach from Gainesville was stopped at East Belknap, twenty miles east of here, and the driver compelled to cut open the mail bags. This is the fourth time the mail has been robbed by road agents on this route.

How Mitchell was Killed.

SAN FRANCISCO, October 20.—A Bakerfield dispatch says that Deputy-Sheriff Mitchell, who was shot by a mob last night, met the crowd as they approached the jail. Nearly all of them were drunk. Shots were at once exchanged, and Mitchell was almost instantly killed. He shot one of his assailants. The crowd then dispersed without accomplishing their object, that of lynching Herbert.

Missouri Train Robbers.

St. Louis, October 20.—At Independence John Bugler and John Land were arraigned in the Criminal Court, upon indictments charging them with participation in the Chicago and Alton train robbery. Both pleaded not guilty, and their trials were postponed until the next term of the court. Bail was fixed at $4200 each. Creed Chapman, one of the leaders of the gang, will be arraigned Saturday.

On the Ground of Insanity.

PHILADELPHIA, October 20.—In the trial of George Wood, charged with throwing vitriol into the face of George Sheppard, by which the latter was terribly burned and lost one eye, the jury returned a verdict of not guilty on the ground of the insanity of the defendant at the time of the commission of the act. The Judge said it remained with him to decide whether Wood should not be confined in an institution for the insane if he has not yet recovered his reason.

The McGrail Murderer.

The McGrain Murderer.

Columbus, O., October 20.—William Bray and John O'Neil have been arrested on suspicion of murdering the soldier, Charles P. McGrail, on Monday morning. Bray was arrested yesterday, but no charge was preferred against him until to-day, when he was accused of murder in the second degree. No charge has been preferred against O'Neil. The murder has caused considerable excitement in this city, which has resulted in severe charges against some members of the police force for neglect of duty.

An Illinois Bank Robbery.

JERSEYVILLE, ILL., October 20.—Charles Clay and John Burrus went into Wesley Park & Sons bank, at Fieldon, at 2 oclock to-day, and at the muzzle of two revolvers compelled Mr. Park to open his safe and give them $5500. The robbers then mounted their horses and rode away. Park followed them to the street and fired upon them, killing one of their horses. The dismounted robber got on the horse of his pal and both of them rode off together. Sheriff Massey raised a posse, and is now scouring the county for the robbers, who it is said cannot escape.

Another Good Man Gone Wreng.

Another Good Man Gone Wrong.

KENOSHA, Wis., October 20.—Herbert Theirs, of this city, has committed forgeries to the amount of $60,000 in mortgages and notes. Among others, he made a duplicate of a mortgage on E. Pennoyer for $14,000, and played the same trick on others in amounts of three and four thousand dollars. A number of other misdeeds have been discovered. He left town at noon to-day, and early in the afternoon the entire matter was discovered. He was a highly respected member of one of the Kenosha churches. No trace of him has yet been discovered.

An Arkansas Episode.

An Arkansas Episode.

HELENA, ARK., October 20.—Three negroes have been arrested at Oldtown Ridge, charged with the murder of an overseer named McMath. They were taken by a masked mob from the guard, and James Cunningham, one of them, was shot and left for dead, but turned up alive and handcuffed the next day, denying his guilt and implicating white men in the murder. A posse is after the mob.—A later dispatch gives the following particulars of the affair: "As W. B. Lindsey, Deputy-Sheriff, and Constable Cole, of Searcy township, and Messrs. Sollivan and Spears, special officers, were returning from Esquire Brand's court last night about 8:30 o'clock with James Cunningham, Henry Lamar and Willie Cunningham, the men charged with the attempted assassination of J. W. McMath, when near Pillow's Bridge, were charged upon by a mob of fifty men. As the mob rushed upon them Officer Lindsey drew his pistol and ordered them to halt, but was immediately confronted by three men with shotguns and ordered to keep quiet. The mob then took the prisoners from the wagon to the side of the road, and told Jim Cunningham to confess before they shot him. He replied that he was innocent. Then several volleys were fired at him and he was left for dead. The other two prisoners were returned to the custody of the officers, who brought them to the city and lodged them in jail. The men were disguised and but one or two spoke a word, so that it was impossible to recognize any of them. This morning Esquire Burnett summoned a jury and proceeded to the scene to hold an inquest. Arriving on the ground he found the body of Cunningham gone, but, after a search, it was found three-quarters of a mile distant, having crawled that distance in the dark. The physicians report that the wound of Cunningham is not dangerous, and he was jailed. He has made a statement, charging several parties with shooting him, and warrants have been issued for their arrests. It is thought that all of them can prove an alibi. Cunningham seems to be bullet-proof, having been shot and left for dead several years ago."

Among our State Exchanges.
The Morehouse Clarion says that it has not rained enough in that place in three months to wet the ground an inch deep. It has been longer than that since we had that much rain.

The complaint of drought still continues to be general almost entirely throughout the State.

Mallison Journal: The merchants are beginning to put on a cheerful look as they can now see the fleecy article beginning rapidly to come in to our market, with a good prospect ahead and plenty to supply all the crop around this vicinity. Good stocks of goods are being daily received, and customers from all quarters will be able to meet with bargains.

A beef belonging to Mr. Goldburg, in its efforts to escape the slaughter pen, took to the Mississippi river, just above the waist of boat and was not captured until it had swam down the river opposite Mrs. Bigg's plantation, being at least six miles below where it first struck the river.

Baton Rouge Capriolian: The stone work on the State House commenced Monday, and the workmen are pushing the work forward with a vim that is commendable. We understand that the working force will be increased as fast as possible.

The rain! oh the glorious rain! It fell yester day in sufficient quantities to lay the dust, cool the atmosphere and refresh the people and things generally. We feel better, and we are certain every body looks livelier and brighter. God bless the rain, and give us a little more.

Clinton Watchman: Henry Norwood a colored man living in this parish, nine miles north of Clinton, who with team and wagon loaded with freight while on his way from Bayon Sara to Rose Hill, when crossing, and about the middle of the bridge spanning the Comite River near the residence of Mrs. James, the bridge gave way and the loaded wagon, team and driver went down into the water, breaking the thigh bone of one horse and shoulder bones of one mule. The driver and Mr. Norwood, himself, came out with a few bruises. The wagon was but slightly injured. It was a narrow escape from death by the men.

St. Martinsville Observer: Two dastardly attempts were made Tuesday during the night to fire the stores of M. M. Knight and Millot. The fiends, after perforating the doors, saturated the floor with coal oil and ignited it. Fortunately the smoke that filled the rooms awoke the inmates who succeeded in extinguishing the flames. Had the dastards succeeded in their attempts, our town in all probability would now be in ashes, as the buildings fired are situated in the most thickly settled part of the town, and where the buildings are all frame and only a few feet apart. The scarcity of water would have rendered it impossible to contend successfully against the flames with the brisk breeze blowing at the time. These attempts had a de moralizing effect on the people, and indignation ran high. We still remember the terrible fire of 1855, the work of an incendiary, which cost the lives of fourteen persons, and which swept away the entire business portion of the town. It were well that our citizens should take prompt measures to escape another like scourge. Although we do not favor high handed measures, we do not hesitate in this case to advise the people, if the fiends are detected, to apply immediately to Judge Lynch's Court for immediate redress.

joe-caleb-vernon-1881-08-31.A8:
LOUISIANA LYNCH-LAW.
The Columbia Herald gives particulars of a case of incendiarism in Jackson parish. The residence of Mr. Fuller was set on fire last April, while thirteen persons were in the house—coal oil having been poured here and there to facilitate the work of conflagration. Two colored persons, a man and a woman, were subsequently arrested on suspicion; and the evidence against the man was very strong. He broke jail and escaped before indictment; and the jury failed to agree as to the guilt of the woman, there being eleven for conviction and one for acquittal. Subsequently in the latter part of August the fugitive negro was rearrested, taken out of jail by a mob, and hung to a tree.

The crime was a peculiarly fiendish one, for all the inhabitants of the house might have been burnt alive. The evidence was strong against the lynched negro; and there is every probability that had he been tried, he might have been acquitted through the stupidity or partizanship of a mixed jury. But it is nevertheless to be deprecated that such a course should have been pursued until his guilt was settled beyond all shadow of doubt. And there are always schemers ready and eager to coin political capital out of such occurrences.

But it must be remembered that in certain parts of Louisiana the whites must rule with a rod of iron in order to preserve law and order. In Jackson there is a small white majority; but there are parishes in which the black majority is enormous. The two great crimes to which the blacks are most prone under the influence of passion are rape and arson; crimes which ought in all civilized countries to be invariably punished with death. Then there is the cause of the jury farce. A mixed jury will seldom convict a negro of a serious offense, when that offense has been perpetrated against some one not of their own color. But law must nevertheless hold its own: and the ignorant mass of negroes must learn that the intelligent portion of the population in their parish can rule, and will be masters, and will enforce the penalties of the law in spite of the abnormal condition of affairs. Therefore, while it is possible that the lynchers of the incendiary in Jackson acted overhastily, we can hardly blame them if they were positive that they had the right man.

In a few years more, however, there will be an end of such scandals and such horrors; but the black population will sink to a natural level of numerical inferiority. The parishes will be thickly settled; men from the North and East and West will pour into Louisiana, while from the South Spanish and French emigration will swell the white population. Until an increase of population and capital, and a consequent increase of prosperity, law will be so well established that the public need not fear that any such crimes as rape and arson will be suffered to go unpunished by the courts. It is the distrust of legal authority that often leads unauthorized men, as it did in the above case, to take law into their own hands. N. O. Item.

W. M. Carpenter, charged with the murder of Tully W. Orr, on the 27th of January, in the parish of Morehouse, has been tried and acquitted.

George Oscar was shot and killed by George Decker, a restaurant keeper at Pleasant Hill station, on the New Orleans Pacific railroad, DeSoto parish. Oscar refused to pay for a cigar and fired two shots at Decker, who returned the fire with fatal effect.

A colored man named Joe Synagogue, Jr., accidently shot himself while returning from a hunt, at Holmesville, parish of Avoyelles. A load of fifteen buckshot struck him under the chin, breaking his neck and almost blowing his head off.

A crowd of colored men numbering fifty or sixty engaged in a drunken row at Tangipahoa, during which sticks, knives and other weapons were freely used and three men seriously wounded. About fifteen of the rioters were arrested, all but two of whom were released on bail.

Jonas Daniels, a colored resident of Tangipahoa parish, buried a bucket of specie on his premises. His stepson, Johnny Taylor, found the treasure, took a handful of the money and told Ike Solomons of it. Ike lost no time in getting away with the rest of the wealth. A special election was held in Madison parish on the 10th ultimo to decide whether a special levee tax of five mills should be levied. The vote was almost unanimously in favor of the tax, viz: 220 for, 12 against.

Carroll Jones, a colored farmer in Natchitoches parish, has 350 acres of magnificent cotton, doubtless the finest in the State. Experts among Mr. Jones' neighbors have certified that 80 acres will yield at least two bales to the acre, and that "it actually beats any thing we have ever seen in the cotton line."

Hon. H. R. Steele, President of the proposed Natchez, Vitalia and Sabine railroad, telegraphs from New York that he has secured sufficient capital to construct the entire line.

Rev. Elias George, an old citizen of Tangipahoa, had his skull fractured and right hip broken in the recent accident on the Vicksburg and Meridian railroad near Edwards, Miss. His condition is critical.
Josh Woodruff, colored, was shot and killed at a ball on T. K. Smith's plantation, in Grant parish. There are conflicting reports as to the identity of the man who did the shooting.

Mrs. Polk, daughter of Hon. Hiram R. Lott of West Carroll, committed suicide by taking an overdose of morphine. The unfortunate lady was a sister of the young men who were recently killed by Deputy Sheriff Sage in the streets of Lloyd. Col. Lott has the universal sympathy of the community in his terrible triple bereavement.

Hardy Price, a colored thief, entered the corn field of Mr. G. A. Zahn, near Baton Rouge, during the night, and while in the act of helping himself to corn was shot and killed by Mr. Zahn.

A proposition to extend the corporate limits of Mansfield was defeated by a vote of two to one at a special election held for the purpose of deciding the question.

A colored man named Louis Johnson was picked up on the railroad track near Mansfield, with two severe wounds on his head, which may prove fatal. It is supposed he fell from a train.

CRIMES AND CASUALTIES.
Boiler Explosion at Jersey City--Mysterious Disappearance--Why Murderers Are Lynched in Arkansas.
MISSING.
A St. Joseph special says: The fourth or fifth mysterious disappearance within a year has just taken place. The missing man is Walter C. Bailey, shipping clerk in the house of Turner, Frisco & Co. He disappeared last Tuesday and has not been heard of since. He was suffering from a temporary aberration of the brain, probably produced by malerial fever. Last Tuesday he attempted to shoot a lady and gentleman in the St. Charles hotel, and fired, but the ball passed through the clothing of the persons. The revolver was taken from him. He demanded it two or three times but it was refused. Since then nothing has been seen or heard of him.

FEARFUL EXPLOSION.

JERSEY CITY, Sept. 13.—A bay boiler exploded this morning at Bulman & Brown's dock at the foot of Essex street. Capt. Decker, of the tug Gladwish, and Jas. Tamman, were instantly killed, and two or three others fatally injured. The boiler was blown 600 feet up Essex street. In its course it cut down a lamp post and five hydrants. Two large trees and two wagons standing in the street were entirely destroyed. A horse and cart of John Adam's which his son, aged 11, was driving, was struck by the flying boiler, the vehicle and horse literally cut to pieces, and the boy's right leg severed from his body. Cause of explosion, carelessness.

ARKANSAS LYNCHERS JUSTIFIED.

LITTLE Rock, Ark., Sept. 13.—News is received that Saturday night a hundred men rode to the jail at Dorbanville, and took the two murderers, Taylor and Bruce, dragged them into the woods with ropes about their necks and to a patch of timber, where they left them dangling to trees. The men were bruised and lifeless before they reached the scene of their death. Both died defying their executioners. This sort of thing is becoming common in this section and public opinion is with the lynchers, owing to the loose administration of justice in the courts.

HIGHWAYMEN IN NEW ENGLAND.

PORTLAND, Mc., Sept. 13.—A family has been robbed by highwaymen while proceeding from the Glen house to the Thorn Mountain house, near the line of the Portland & Ogdensburg railway. Later the Glen stage coach was fired into but the driver whipped up horses and escaped. Officers are searching for the highwaymen.
john-taylor-dardanelle-1881-09-10.A20:
TWO MURDERERS HUNG.
We are informed that Messrs. Taylor and Bruce, of Yell county, were both taken from the Dardaneille jail on Saturday night and hung. This is a terrible precedent and opens the door for unauthorized and arbitrary violence and merits the condemnation of all good law abiding citizens. The long delays by the courts, the very many technicalities of the law so common and invariably resorted to for postponing the trial of criminals, the injudicious and too frequently extended clemency of the pardoning power of the executive, the many escapes from the jails of the country, together with the wholesale delivery by the sheriff or guard (the very officers of the law whose duty it was to keep secure and not to liberate) from the Ozark jail so many men and prisoners who had in cold blood murdered Burgess James in Yell county, entailing in addition to this horrible and atrocious deed upon her citizens, a very large, heavy and extraordinary bill of costs in their prosecution, all of which has doubtless for the reasons and causes enumerated been the incentive to action of those engaged in this objectionable and arbitrary tragedy and which it is said from rumor was composed of some of the very best and heretofore law abiding citizens of Yell county. Until a different course shall be pursued by the courts in giving speedier trials, the abandonment of technicalities resorted to by attorneys for delays and postponements, and less extension and clemency of the pardoning power of the executive of the state, with a more rigid care and safe keeping of prisoners by officers of the law, whose duty it is to secure and not liberate them, we need not expect a correction or abandonment of the greatly to be deplored evils of mob violence and lynch law.

CRIME.
Ex-Minister Christianity was robbed of $6,000 worth of diamonds and jewelry in his strong box in his room, in the National hotel, Washington. The thieves forced the door and secured the plunder during Christianity's temporary absence. The jewels were not the property of Christianity, but left with him for safe-keeping. It is believed the thieves followed Christianity from New York.

It is claimed that six of the Glendale train-robbers have been captured. They prove to be young farmers living in the immediate vicinity of the outrage, and the idea that the James brothers were in the raid has been quite generally abandoned. Matt Chapman gave to a sheriff the names of the robbers, and has himself been placed in jail at Independence as a witness.

A party of armed and mounted men took from the jail at Dardenelle, Ark, two murders named John Taylor and J. F. Bruce, and hanged them in an adjacent grove. The reason of the lynching was that the prisoners were likely to escape justice by changes of venue.

Two young planters of Booneville, Ark, named William and Robert Hambery, were shot by parties in ambush along the roadside. The latter was instantly killed and the former mortally wounded. Two negroes have been arrested on suspicion.

Jane Campbell, a colored woman living near Dycke's Mills, La., killed her two children, aged 10 and 12, by beating their brains out with pine knots for some trivial act of disobedience. A mob took the woman from jail and burned her at the stake.

Maurice C. Stettheimer, who occupied a confidential position in the office of Messrs. Seligman, bankers of New York, has been lodged in the Tombs for embezzling $40,000. He was traced to Sault Ste. Marie by detectives.

A moonshine distillery, of the most primitive pattern, which has probably been in operation for the past two months, was discovered in a ravine in the northern part of Parke county, Indiana.

Three masked burglars visited the house of a hermit at Collinsville, O., named John McCavarry, bound him to his bed, and compelled him to reveal the hiding-place of $6,000 in currency.

At Philadelphia, Pa., Herman C. Pulte, the Whitaker will conspirator, used as a witness for the commonwealth, was sentenced by Judge Mitchell to three years imprisonment.

Clem Gallion, of Cambridge, Ill., was executed for the murder of an old man named Dilley last December. He died in about seven minutes.

Harry Mordaunt, charged with felony while being taken from San Francisco to Portland in irons, sprang overboard and was lost to view.

A mob at Owingsville, Ky., took Samuel Ramsay from jail and hanged him for murder.
john-taylor-dardanelle-1881-09-10.A34:
MOB LAW.
It is with a great deal of regret that we observe the growing popularity of Judge Lynch in our State. His visits are becoming so frequent as to excite solicitude in the breast of all good citizens. Week before last his terrible power was exerted upon a victim in Jackson county, and also in Yell county his swift judgement was visited upon two. We are not thoroughly posted as to the details of the crimes charged against any of the parties, but do not think from our information that they were of that agravated form which somehow or other it meets with partial public favor to visit with such swift and condign punishment outside the forms of law.

It has never been eradicated from the minds of the people to wreak vengeance upon certain base and wicked crimes committed in their midst, but in our country the exercise of this frightful power has been principally confined to the few cases that shock public morals and outrage the principles of virtue. The cases before us are exceptions to this rule. They fell in the line of murder—a crime which is dark and wicked, 't is true, but one which has always been accorded a hearing and final adjudication in the courts, and we know of nothing in any of these cases that would take them out of the line of crimes of this sort. The inquiry then arises, what is the matter, and where is the trouble?

Is the fault with the people? We are loth to believe it. They have possibly allowed themselves to some extent to be thrown into a state of solicitude by the tardiness of justice in our courts in which they have come to think that public safety lies in their dealing out to criminals that which lies in the jurisdiction of courts to give, but which they have been so prone of late to escape. What the people want, and what they demand, is that crime shall be punished. And we look upon these occurrences not so much as a spirit of mob law, as an attestation of this def mand. The heavy cost of criminal prosecution, the endless delays of justice and the final escape of the criminal, have conspired to make justice a byword and punishment for crime a mockery. In this state of the case, much as we may regret it, it is not surprising that occasionally the feeling should show itself beyond the limits of prudence, to enforce obedience to the demand that the law must be enforced.

It's an unpleasant sentence to write in which responsibility for this state of feeling is placed anywhere, and especially with those in whose hands is the administration of law. We think, however, that we take no risk in the proposition that with a vigorous, speedy and certain execution of the law, our eyes would never have seen the particulars of these occurrences.

mcdougall-marinette-1881-10.A9:
Murder and Lynch Law.
Frank and John McDonald, two ex-convicts who have just completed an eighteen-months' term in the State prison, and have been out only two weeks, while at a disreputable house in the outskirts of this village, day before yesterday, got into a row with Willie Kittson, a half-breed, about 23 years old. Norman Kittson and one Tommy Dunn went to the relief of Willie, and took him from the house and started for home. The McDonalds followed them and attacked them again on the street. Willie was knocked down and then stabbed several times. Norman received several severe knife wounds in the face and side. Willie died within a few moments after receiving his wounds, and Norman can not live. The McDonalds were promptly arrested by Sheriff Barclay and lodged in the county jail, where they remained until last evening. Great excitement prevailed from the time of the murder, and extra guards were placed over the jail. About 10 o'clock last night a mob of over 500 people, composed mostly of Frenchmen, Indians and half-breeds, approached the jail, overpowered the Sheriff and guard, and with heavy timbers, sledgehammers and axes broke open the door of the jail and of the cell where the McDonalds were lodged. The prisoners were pulled out of the cell and long ropes fastened about their necks, and they were then dragged by the mob mercilessly through the street for three-quarters of a mile to the house where the row originated, where their bodies were suspended to a tree. The victims were dead, however, long before their bodies were hung up. The house above mentioned was then set on fire and burned to the ground. The two bodies were left suspended to the tree until this morning, when they were taken down by the authorities. When the jail was attacked, a large number of citizens responded promptly to the call of the Sheriff for help, but the mob had obtained entrance to the jail, and resistance was then impossible.
