FROM OUR STATE EXCHANGES
manie, has a squash on exhibition which weighs 182 pounds.

Advices from muskrats in various portions of the state are that they are building for a mild winter.

Gilbert Curtis, of Racine, was killed at Delevan on the 8th, while engaged in switching cars.

A child aged seventeen months died at Oconto a few days ago from the effects of drinking concentrated lye.

The Wisconsin Cedar Post Company, of Cavoits, for the purpose of traffic in telegraph posts, railroad ties and cedar posts, has been incorporated.

The United States troops who were ordered to Shawano some time since to suppress an anticipated Indian outbreak, have been ordered back to Fort Snelling.

John Collins, employed in a Racine tannery, was so badly injured by machinery on the 11th that he will lose an arm.

A lamp explosion at Brooklyn, N. Y., caused the loss of eyesight to I. G. Hatch, formerly a well-known jeweler of Oshkosh.

A young man of 21 years, Samuel M. Stanton, a medical student, was drowned at Hudson on the 10th, while swimming after a duck which he had shot.

Burglars entered the store of Jacob Noll, Sturgeon Bay, recently, during the temporary absence of the owner, and stole money and goods to the amount of $120.

Reports of damage by the flood still continue from Wausau, Rochester, Merrill, Waupaca and other places. At Wausau the river has reached the high-
A terrific stroke of lightning, during a recent thunder-storm at Tomah, struck a school house and injured several children. The lightning, passing outside, uprooted trees and plowed furrows in the ground for a distance of six rods.

Articles of association of the Star Prairie (St. Croix County) Manufacturing Company, with a capital of $10,000, have been filed with the secretary of state. The company will manufacture wagons, carriages, sleighs and various farm implements.

Monroe Sentinel: A little girl, three and a halt years old, child of R. Buri, of this place fell into a tub of hot water recently, and was scalded so badly that she died a few hours after the accident. The child's sufferings were terrible, and the parents are almost distracted.

The west side of the building occupied by the Free Press Company, at Eau Claire, through the undermining of the foundations by the recent floods, fell on the 12th, causing a loss of $2,500 to the printing company and $1,500 to the owners of the building.

Rev. J. W. McCormick, of Waupaca, recently invited to resign by the M. E. Conference on account of heresy, has been tendered and has accepted a call for an independent pastorate made by the liberal-minded Christians of Waupaca, with a salary of $1,000 a year.

Frank Utley, who has been confined in the penitentiary at Waupun for the
FRANK UTLEY, who has been confined in the penitentiary at Waupun for the murder of his father, in Green Lake County, made his escape on the 12th, and is still at large. He was at work in the garden with several other convicts, and was not missed until some time after he had taken his departure.

NELSON W. ALDRICH, recently chosen to succeed the late Ambrose E. Burnside as United States senator from Rhode Island, is related to Congressman Aldrich of Chicago, and to J. F. Aldrich of Fond du Lac, predecessor to Mann Brothers, of Milwaukee, in the extensive business they now carry on.

NICHOLAS OPP, of Oshkosh, aged 39, is under arrest for attempting rape on a child of 6 years. The child is said to be considerably injured. The child's mother is said to have caught Opp in the act, and attempted to shoot him. Opp, however, claims that the whole case is one of blackmail.

A NUMBER of the party which lynched the McDonald cousins, at Marinette have been arrested, among them the ringleader, Forvilly. The father of one of the boys is active in the case. He is worth about $300,000, and says he is willing to spend his last dollar to see justice done. A brother of the elder McDonald worth as much more, expresses the same views.

GREEN BAY Advocate: Last Sunday a shower of spider webs fell here. They came apparently from the upper air. We noticed them at noon and they were certainly falling for as much as two hours. The webs varied from 50 to 60 feet long to mere specks and could be seen as far up in the air as the eye could reach. From any one stand-point a person could count a dozen of them at one time. Over how large a tract of country it extended we have no means of judging, but certainly all over this city and Fort Howard, and we hear of it three miles east, at the Vosburgh place. At the latter place the webs fell so thick as to seriously annoy the horses by getting in their eyes. The webs we examined were a snow white and very strong.
mcdougall-marinette-1881-10.A13:
FROM OUR STATE EXCHANGES
A MOVEMENT is on foot looking toward the establishment of a sewing machine factory in La Crosse.

OLE NELSON, aged 80 years, a resident of Racine, received fatal injuries on the 26th, by falling down stairs.

MRS. AUGUSTA RADELL, a well-known young lady of Palmyra, died on the 22d, aged 25 years.

It is now stated that the name of one of the two cousins recently lynched at Marinette was McDougall instead of McDonald.

L. M. REESE, examined at Madison for complicity in the recent burglary at Waunakee, has been held to bail in the sum of $1,000.

A FRENCHMAN named Jaloit was drowned on the 22d by falling through the floor of a saw-mill into the river at Chippewa Falls.

WILLIAM POWERS, a brakeman on the Chicago, Milwaukee and St. Paul Railway, was killed at La Crosse on the 23d, while coupling cars.

EDWARD R. EVANS, a well-known liveryman of Watertown, died on the 25th, from the effects of injuries received in a runaway accident on Saturday last.

A MAN named Martin Hoffman, six miles north of Oshkosh, committed suicide on the 24th by hanging. The cause was temporary aberration of mind.

The body of E. M. Brown, a night watchman at the harbor at Sheboygan, who had been missing since October 5, has been found floating outside the harbor.

HUGO WERTHMAN's store and stock of
Hugo Werthman's store and stock of goods at Green Bay were damaged by fire on the 25th to the amount of $2,000. The cause of the fire was a defective chimney.

Ex-Governor Fairchild has recently written from Madrid to friends in Wisconsin, that he will spend the coming winter at some resort in southern Europe.

William Stumm, a special watchman of the Chicago and North-Western Railway at Baraboo, was killed by a train on the 22d. It is supposed that he went to sleep while sitting on the track.

A boy of eight years, name not given, was drowned at Snell's Station a day or two ago through the sudden flooding of the family residence. Other members of the family escaped with difficulty.

The water at Appleton, Neenah, Oshkosh, Stevens Point, Fond du Lac and other places is still very high, and apprehensions of danger are still felt. The Mississippi at La Crosse is falling rapidly.

Articles of incorporation have been filed by the Oshkosh Carriage Company, comprising the creditors of Parson & Goodfellow, of Oshkosh. The works will be run on a larger scale than even. The capital is $125,000.

The remains of a man named Reese Davis were found in Tomah recently, lying in a ditch near the depot. A coroner's jury found that he was accidentally drowned while under the influence of liquor. He was a laboring man.

F. R. Bickenbach, of Freeport, Ill.,
F. R. BICKENBACH, of Freeport, Ill., a brakeman on the Chicago, Milwaukee and St. Paul Railway, was seriously injured by falling from a moving train at Elkhorn, on the 24th. One leg was caught by the wheels and badly mangled.

A small warehouse near the depot at Palmyra, owned by Mrs. Chopin, was burned on the 23d. Lumber worth $2,500, belonging to J. E. Gregory was also burned by the same fire. There was no insurance on any of the property. The fire was incendiary.

High water still continues at Oshkosh, and the flood is spreading. The manufacturers are investigating a report that this is partly due to the Neenah mill men raising their dam to secure greater water power. In case this is found to be true, actions for damage will be commenced.

Miss Etta Judd, a well-known young lady of Monroe, through the sudden opening of a door recently, had a lamp, which she was carrying, smashed. The oil was scattered over her clothing and she was so badly burned that she is not expected to live. Her clothing was almost entirely burned from her person.

Medina correspondence Oshkosh Northwestern: Daniel Lieby, a young man residing in Dale, fell dead the 18th inst. The family except young Leiby and sister were away from the home. His sister had gone down cellar, but upon hearing a scream from her brother rushed up stairs to find him a corpse. He had been in usual health excepting an injury upon the knee about three weeks previous, but this was not supposed to be anything serious.

WILLIAM DETTERICK, an old bachelor of Beloit, a German, was attacked in his cabin recently by two young men, who, after knocking him down with an axe, tied his legs together, covered him with bankets and left him for dead. The attack was made for the purpose of robbery, though the robbers got nothing of value save a watch, which they dropped in their haste. The old man, who is a railway flag-man, has nearly recovered from his injuries. Two young men, McKevitt and Gilbert, have been arrested for the crime. McKevitt was identified by Dettrick as one of his assailants, though stoutly protesting innocence.

Traveling Turners.
NEW YORK, May 31.—Three hundred Turners from New York and other cities leave by special train tomorrow for St. Louis where the 23d festival of the North American Turner Bundis to be held beginning on Saturday and ending the following Wednesday. The members of the turner societies accompany the party. On their return receptions will be given the party at Cincinnati, Cumberland and Washington.

Struck By Lightening.
KNIGHTSTOWN, Ind., June 1—1 d.m.—During a heavy storm last evening, the bagging factory of Joen Caseley and son was struck by lightening, and entirely consumed. Loss $25,000, insurance $12,000. Seventy hands thrown out of employment.

Unusual Drought.
CINCINNATI, May 31.—An unusual drought for so early in the spring prevails throughout this section. No rain has fallen for nearly three weeks, and crops are beginning to parch. Barley and wheat, which are now heading out, are materially injured and unless rain falls soon corn, wheat, oats and berries will suffer severely.

Mrs. Abraham Lincoln Dying.
SPRINGFIELD, Ills., May 31.—All hopes for the recovery of Mrs. Lincoln, the widow of Abraham Lincoln, have been abandoned. She daily grows weaker and her attending physicians say she cannot survive many days longer.

Heavy Burglary.
PAINESVILLE, Ohio, May 31.—The hardware store of Kennedy & Son, at Wilbough, was burglized, and $10,500 in paper and money taken. The door was broken and the safe
Willoughby, was burglarized, and $10,500 in paper and money taken. The door was broken and the safe lock crushed.

A Strange Distemper.
Mount Gilroad, Ohio, May 31—Within the last week an epidemic disease among horses, commencing with symptoms noticeable in cases of distemper and finally going to the brain and causing very sudden death, has begun to rage in Chester and Franklin townships, in the eastern part of this county.

Lew Leaves.
SENTA Fr, N. M., May 31—Gov. Lew Wallace, the new minister to Turkey, has turned his office over to the acting governor, Pitch; and left for Washington to call on President Garfield and Secretary Blaine before departing for Constantinople.

A Ghastly Mystery.
Chicago, May 31—Further stalking discoveries have been made in connection with the severed head and headless corpse of a man found in the woods in a suburb north of this city yesterday. A bundle of clothing consisting of a comforter, hat and coat were discovered, stowed away in a hollow tree where the head was found. The hat and coat were of unusually fine material, but evidently of foreign manufacture. Inside the hat were blood stains and tufts of fine light colored hair. The pockets of the coat contained the cards of a hotel in Bremen, printed in German and Bohemian, and also several little articles that would naturally be carried only by a well-to-do person. The identity of the man is still a mystery. Everything leads to show he was a newly arrived foreigner, and murdered for his money.

Regulator Rule.
CINCINNATI, May 31—4 p. m.—Reports from Carter county, Kentucky, mention the killing of two women and a man named McKinney by the regulators. Other crimes are reported and almost a reign of terror rules in some parts of the country.

A Brutes Suicide.
INDIANAPOLIS, Ind., May 31.—John Enrich, an ex-member of the police made a murderous assault on his wife and father-in-law yesterday, after which he shot himself in the head, dying in a few minutes. His wife had applied for a divorce and fled his house in fear of her life. He shot her twice and her father once but both will recover.

An Editor Jailed.
National Associated Press.
COLUMBUS, O., May 31.—The supreme court has over-ruled the motion for leave to file a petition in error to reverse the judgment of the district court of Cuyahoga county in the case of John P. O'Brien vs. State. O'Brien is editor of The Sunday Times, at Cleveland, and was convicted of publishing obscene literature. He will now go to jail.

Notice. The Woman's Christian Association of Lexington, will meet Tuesday afternoon June 7 at 4 o'clock, in the Ladies Reading-room City Library. All ladies interested in good works are cordially invited to be present. Long Service at City Mission on Sunday next. Killing at Cynthiana. Volney Hall, son of Jesse Hall, of Bourbon county, was shot and killed at Cynthiana at 9 a. m. Tuesday by his brother-in-law, Alex. Oder, a wealthy live stock trader. As he met Hall, he asked, "Are you ready?" and instantly fired a shotgun, Hall falling and receiving a second load after being down. He died instantly. He was aged about 50 years. Hall had eleven buckshot in his left breast where he was first shot, and then his head was nearly torn off by the other barrel. Hall was unarmed. He had treated his wife (Oder's sister) and her several children badly, which was probably the cause of the shooting. Carp. We were shown last Wednesday by Mr. Jno. Hostetter, of this county, probably the largest specimen of carp ever caught out of the waters in this part of the State. It was about fourteen inches long and weighed a little over four pounds. Mr. Hostetter says he put the fish in his pond about two years ago. The Pump Business. Messrs. McCray & Co., our neighbors have sold out their entire stock and interest in the pump business and will hereafter devote their time and attention to Elastic Roofing Messrs. Davidon and Williams were the purchasers and have removed the stock to their present place of business on Short street. Killed with a Washboard. In a negro broil which occurred last Tuesday, in Gill's alley, a small street running between Jefferson and Georgetown streets, above Short, Jo. Smith, a dissolute negro woman, struck Silas Payne, also a negro, on the back of the neck such a blow as to cause dislocation of that part, from the effects of which he died in a few minutes. Harness.
The fame of the harness made by Thompson & Boyd, of this city, has gone abroad. They are filling orders from Conneticut, Pennsylvaina, Chicago, New Orleans and other distant points. The horsemen who come here like the style and fit of their harness better than what they are accustomed to at home, and send orders to have Messrs. Thompson & Boyd make harness for them.

Regulators.

Regulators in Carter county are still engaged in their maraudings. Last week, on Kenney creek, in that county, the family from whom this stream takes its name, was assaulted by these self-constituted correctors of the public morals, and when resistance was offered by the inmates of the house the outlaws fired upon them, killing one man and two women.

Narrow Escape

On Monday night between 9 and 10 o'clock a fire was discovered in the kitchen of Mr. V. K. Glass, which is in the basement of his handsome residence in the country. It was rapidly working its way to the floor above, and soon would have been beyond control. No very great damage was done. It is not known how the fire originated.—Georgetown Time.

STATE NEWS.
The Henderson Reporter pines for a music hall in that city.

A negro man named Sias Penn, dropped dead at Lexington.

Georgetown is to be decorated with flags during commencement week.

A. J. Blake will start a Republican paper at Paducah in a few days.

Rolla Ryan, the elocutionist and facial artist, was at Mayfield last week.

The teachers of the State will meet in convention at Elizabethtown July 12 and 15.

Judge Cofer, held a Policy in the National Mutual Benefit association for $4,000.

Col. Jno. Preston, a prominent Democrat of Triumble county, died last week.

A young man of promise, named Geo. Rehm, fell dead of heart disease at Louisville.
Judge R. C. Bowling has been nominated for the Legislature in Logan county.

Jno. Thompson was killed by lightning at Owensboro, while replanting corn.

Josephine Smith killed Silas Payne her paramour, by striking him with a wash-board at Lexington.

The Herald says Mrs. Sallie Autry. of Ohio county, was attacked and severely mangled by a vicious dog.

A German farmer named Gabriel Guoege near Louisville shot the top of his head off. Cause family troubles.

At Cynthiana, Holney Hull was shot and killed by Alex Odor. There was no provocation to justify the deed.

Ben and Jno Stebbens, two bros. were shot and killed in Henry Co. while attempting to commit a robbery.
The Echo says the P. and E. railroad has been sold to the Chesapeake and Ohio, the sale to take effect August 7th.

Wm. Cunningham killed Jno. Alexander, who had hunted him down, near Paris, and was trying to shoot him.

Ewing Grayham, of Mayfield, did not die from the effects of his self-inflicted wound as reported last week, but is recovering.

A negro boy in Hopkins county shot his sister while fooling with an old gun and inflicted a severe wound, says the Times.

Jno. Graham, a ten-year convict, made a fellow prisoner cut off his hand with an axe to keep from working in the penitentiary.

Jacob Bendel was killed and Fred Meyer fatally hurt by a falling embankment while they were digging a cellar in Louisville.
Thos. R. Woods, son of Dr. Woods, editor of the Glasgow Times, has received an appointment to the West Point Military Academy.

Regulators murdered three persons named McKinney, a man and two women, because they refused to be driven from the country in Carter county.

The Reporter says Canoe Creek waters have turned black and the fish are all dead and floating on the surface. Some attribute it to the locusts while others say the distilleries on the creek cause the trouble.

The Reporter says the jailor of Henderson loaned a dismissed prisoner $1 to leave the country and received a letter from Louisville the other day returning the borrowed money. His name was Barmour.

Kentucky Regulators.
In Carter County, Ky. the work of
In Carter County, Ky., the work of the Regulators, if we can believe an Owingsville correspondent, is being carried on more fiercely than ever, notwithstanding they are reported to have disbanded. On Kinney Creek lives a family named McKinney, consisting of two women and one man. The Regulators last week visited the family, forced an entrance and killed all of them. This is but one instance. A house and barn was burned by them for a man named Smith. Three men were shot and seriously wounded. Several raids have been made in Rowan County, near Hogtown.

Mike Wallis,attempted
Mike Wells, colored, attempted to commit an outrage upon Mrs. J. F. Childs, a highly respected widow lady, yesterday, but failed, having been frightened away by her shrieks. He was trailed by the impression of his feet, which were encased in sacks full of holes, arrested, confessed his crime and was banged by the citizens in the Court House yard, between twelve and one o'clock this morning.

CRIMES AND CASUALTIES-BY TELEGRAPH.
DROWNED IN THE CONNECTICUT RIVER.
SPRINGFIELD, Mass., Aug. 2.—Patrick Shea, son of Murty Shea, of this city, fell from a platform on the bank of the river this afternoon and was drowned.

DROWNED IN NORTH POND, MASS.

WORCESTER, Mass., Aug. 2.—Charles Fish, twenty-eight years old, had a hit while rowing on North Pond today, and fell into the water and was drowned.

A NEGRO LYNCHED FOR ASSAULT.
DYERSBURG, Tenn., Aug. 2.—“Mike” Walls, a negro, was lynched here yesterday upon his confession of having attempted to assault Mrs. J. F. Childers.

A POLICE CAPTAIN MURDERED.
LEXINGTON, Ky., Aug. 2.—Captain C. M. Hendricks, of the police force here, was shot dead yesterday by Charles Steele, a negro liquor-seller, while endeavoring to arrest him. The murderer has been arrested.

SHOT DEAD BY OFFICERS.
DRESDEN, Tenn., Aug. 2.—On Sunday Jordan Thompson, colored, cut a white man with a razor, and fled. He was pursued by officers, who, on his refusal to surrender, shot him dead.

KILLED BY A BOILER EXPLOSION.
PROVIDENCE, R. I., Aug. 2.—The boiler in Smith, Grant & Co.'s coal and lumber yard, at Pawtucket, exploded this morning. Bernard McCudden, the engineer, was blown a distance of forty feet, and instantly killed. He was forty years old, and unmarried.

A FLAGMAN BADLY INJURED.
TRENTON, N. J., Aug. 2.—James D. Hosier, thirty-six years of age, of this city, employed as flagman by the Pennsylvania Railroad Company, at Morrisville, Penn., while flagging one train at that place to-day, was struck by another train and dangerously injured.

STAGE ROBBERY IN TEXAS.
GALVESTON, Tex., Aug. 2.—A special to The News from Uvaide, this State, says: “The east-bound stage was robbed at a point four miles west of here Sunday night. The passengers were not disturbed, but the mails were ransacked.”

MURDESED BY A NEGRO.
WYTHEVILLE, Va., Aug. 2.—At Rea Mountain, Sunday night, in a lonely hut, James Leghorn, a white man, who had just returned from North Carolina, found “Jim” Tabor, a negro, lying with his wife. A fight ensued and Tabor shot Leghorn dead.

CANON CITY Described by a Memphian - A Pretty Good Place, But -.
About eight months ago I bade farewell to your beautiful city, which had been my home for several years. I had determined to "Go West, young man, and grow up with the country." So on the 25th day of November last I found myself dumped off a narrow-gauge coach at the base of the Rockies, in the town of Canon City, Colorado, where I have resided ever since. Canon City lies singly at the base of the Foot Range, whose rugged peaks tower to a hight of 2500 feet above the city, and act as forerunners for the snowy range that lies forty miles beyond. The Arkansas at this point breaks through the mountains and forms the Grand Canon, with its Royal Gorge. The little river, Grape creek, here joins the Arkansas with one of the most beautiful canons on earth. The Arkansas Valley here widens out into one of the most charming and fertile of the Colorado parks. About forty miles to the north towers in majestic grandeur the snowy summit of Pike's Peak. Within two hours walk from Canon City is the Royal Gorge of the Arkansas, whose rock walls rise 2000 feet in perpendicular height. The scenery in the vicinity of Canon City varies from the beautiful and lovely to a sublimity that is perfectly awful. Canon City has a population of about twenty-five hundred souls, and is growing rapidly. Her streets are broad avenues, crossing each other at right angles, and are bordered on either side with trees. Every gutter runs as a constant stream of clear water, which gives fertility to her many gardens. Her buildings are mostly of stone or brick, and are very substantial. The city is supplied with pure water from the never-failing Arkansas, and she expects soon to have her streets and halls lighted with gas or electricity. At present there are in course of construction brick and stone buildings which will aggregate a cost of $100,000. The mineral springs of Canon City, in medicinal properties, are not excelled by any in the State. Her soda and

iron springs are almost ice cold, while the hot springs afford a most delicious bath. No place in the United States enjoys a finer and more health-giving climate than Canon City. Her winter days are more like spring than winter, while the summer is never oppressive. It is true that this climate is subject to great and sudden changes, but the extreme dryness, purity and lightness of the atmosphere prevent any serious effect on the human system. Indeed, Canon City has long been a favorite winter resort for the mountaineer, as well as a summer resort for the States. Her altitude of 5000 feet above the sea level tempers the summer heat, and the lofty mountains, to the west and north, softens the rigor of her winters. The region to which Canon City looks for support, and which will, sooner or later, make her a beautiful city, I will set forth in another communication. For the present I will only say that Colorado is not without objections, and I would advise no Tennessee to sacrifice or dispose of a comfortable home with the expectation of finding a better here. What is a paradise for some is a hell for others.

W. J. MILLER.

CHEROKEES

Dropping Into the Political Methods of the Whites.

Special to the Appeal.]

LITTLE ROCK, August 2.—The Indians in the Cherokee Nation, Indian Territory, held a general election yesterday, and selected forty members of the National Council and seventeen of the Grand Council, all for two years. A solicitor, judge and sheriff were also elected in each of the nine districts. There were two tickets—National and Union—in the field, but, in fact, no difference in the platform of the parties, the struggle being the "outs" against the "ins." The returns indicate that the offices are about equally divided. Considerable excitement prevailed, and there were many rows, but no killing. The newly-elected members of the National and Grand Councils will begin their terms of office on the first Monday in November.

WILL THEY NEVER LEARN

That Almost Certain Death Awalts Perpetration of the Crime?

RUTHERFORD, TENN., August 2.—On Sunday night, in the town of Dyersburg, Tennessee, between 12 and 1 o'clock, Mike Wells, colored, entered the house of Mrs. Childs, widow of J. F. Childs, and endeavored to ravish her in the most cruel manner, choking her severely and smothering her with his hands to keep her from giving any alarm; but before he accomplished his hellish intent she succeeded in giving an alarm, which frightened the villain and brought to her rescue a young man who was rooming close by her residence. By this time the scoundrel had made his escape. The young man hastily notified the police force, which by 4 o'clock yesterday morning, headed by Ex-Sheriff Nichols, succeeded in arresting the criminal, who was placed under guard until between 10 and 11 o'clock, when he was taken possession of by an indignant mob, who meted out to him in the Courthouse yard that punishment he so justly deserved, and there he hung to a limb until he was dead, dead, dead.

MASTERS MAY KICK,

But Go to Perryville He Must, as Churchill Says So.

LITTLE ROCK, August 2.—There is no fresh news concerning the military movement in Perryville. Additional troops reached there at 11 o'clock to-day. A message, just received, requests the Governor to have Masters, who was with Matthews when he was killed, sent up at once. Another message says witnesses are afraid to testify, and from this it would seem that there is some difficulty in executing the law in Perryville. Masters will refuse to go, as he is intimidated, but the Governor is requested to send him at all hazards.

LATE NEWS ITEMS.
The New York Herald publishes statistics showing that there has been subscribed in the North and in Europe for investment in the South during the last eighteen months, $100,000,000. Most of this money has been put into the States east of the Mississippi and in the country south of Richmond. It has gone mainly, of course, into railroads. But $2,000,-000 has lately been invested in cotton factories in Augusta alone; and considerable sums have been lent to planters and to mercantile or industrial enterprises.

It is rumored the British officials obtained their information regarding the contemplated shipment of infernal machines from America from a memorandum-book found in possession of McGrath, one of the men indicted for the attempt to blow up the Town Hall at Liverpool.

Ex-Governor George Saulsbury, of Delaware, is dead.

The Colorado Iron Works at Denver, with nearly all the machinery, burned on the 1st. Loss, $125,000; insurance, $41,500.

At Lexington, Ky., Capt. C. M. Hendricks, of the police force, was shot dead in attempting to arrest Charles Steele, a negro saloon-keeper. Steele was arrested.

The Vicksburg quarantine station has been re-established.

Two Indianapolis roughs, John and Thomas Carney, assaulted a car-driver named Wm. Collier, who drew a revolver and fired two shots, killing both. The shooting is considered justifiable.

The Yorktown Centennial celebration will begin on Oct. 18.

By the explosion of fire-damp at the Phoenix Park Colliery, at Pottsville, Pa., John T. Welch and Edward Brady, miners, and Michael Moore and Jas. Brown were badly burned. Welch was a labor reform representative in the last Legislature.

At Dyersburg, Tenn., on the 2d, Mike Wells, a negro, was lynched upon his confessing an assault upon the person of Mrs. J. T. Childress.

At Valley Station, Ky., Geo. M. Alsop, accused of forgery, and a hard case generally, killed Constable J. S. Harrison, who was attempting to arrest him. The murderer had not been captured at last accounts.

H. Andrews, a young farmer living northeast of Marion, Iowa, was thrown from a wagon and killed by the team running away. His body was found by the roadside.

While Mrs. John Cooperrider was engaged in working about a red-hot stove, near Decatur, Ill., her clothes caught fire and she was so badly burned that 'she died in great agony a few hours later. She leaves a husband and one child.

Shreveport Times: We yesterday met Mr. Willie Gilmer, who is employed on the line of the New Orleans Pacific road. He informs us that the track is laid as far as Mount Pleasant, and the work is progressing at the rate of about a mile a day. His account of the condition of many farmers in that section is deplorable—scarcely any corn, cotton vegetables, milk, poultry or money.

Morehouse Clarion: Crops are wofully short in this parish, of both corn and cotton, and it is safe to say that there will not be more than a third of a crop of each made. It is said to be the poorest crop ever made in the parish, and we presume it is true. On our richest land in many places the cotton will not average more than two feet high with from five to ten bolls on a stalk, where formerly it grew as high as a man's head. The fields have burned up under the parching sun with no rain. The drouth set in here early in June, and we have not had a good rain since—an unprecedented dry spell of nearly three months. It looks really distressing, and whilst this is generally true throughout the State, we can't see why the city papers report the crop nearly as good as that of last pear. It is not true, and the facts ought to be given.

Richland Beacon: Some parties in the 5th ward of Morehouse parish, if reports are true, are entitled to credit for the discovery of a new and original mode of punishing a cow thief. It is said that a negro was caught in the act of butchering a cow in the woods, and the parties detecting him cut a small hole in the cow, took out its entrails, put the negro in the cavity and sewed up the hole, leaving only his head out. He had an awful time in keeping the crows from picking his eyes out, and was almost completely exhausted when discovered and released from his uncomfortable quarters by two other negroes.

Richland Beacon: From the mail carrier we learn that another colored man was shot, and it was thought mortally wounded, at Charlieville, last Monday. There is no telling where this murdering business will end, if the murderers now at large are not arrested and brought to justice.

Columbia Herald: On Tuesday morning last about 2 A. M. two negro men, who were lying in Monroe jail under a charge of the murder of two of their race, were taken out by persons unknown and hanged. The keys of the jail were looked up in a desk, in the sheriff's office, the deputy sheriff being at the time absent on duty. The lynching party entered the office, broke open the sheriff's desk, took therefrom the jail key, unlocked the cell in which the negroes were confined and conveyed them some distance out of the town and hanged them without raising any alarm. So quietly and methodically was this thing done that not a soul in the town seems to have either heard or seen anything of the party.

Two weeks ago we published a statement made by the Richland Beacon to the effect that a colored cow-thief had been fastened up in the cavity of a disemboweled cow and remained in that condition until released by some parties passing by. The Beacon stated that this occurred in the 5th ward of this parish. Several reliable citizens of that ward request us to deny the charge. They say, that while they do not condemn the mode of punishment alleged to have been inflicted, they do protest against the accusation of cow-stealing in their ward. For the protection of the name of their ward they wish it understood that the Beacon was misinformed as to the geography of the bovine tragedy. We are glad the fifth can vindicate herself from the charge. The tortures that the buzzards gave the thief while occupying the position of a cow's paunch, can be regarded none the less excruciating, no matter if he was a thousand miles from the fifth ward. Wherever it took place, it was a cow-PITAL mode of punishment.

The Beacon must not accuse this parish of theft falsely. Richland was doubtless the scene of action.

WINCHESTER, February 16—A fervish

The Owl Hollow Murders.

WINCHESTER, February 16.—A feverish state of feeling existed here this afternoon on the arrival of John and Fish Poe, who are alleged to have murdered a man named Baker at Owl Hollow a few nights ago and robbed his store. The general impression prevailed that they are guilty of the crime and that they would be lynched on reaching here. They were under the custody of such a strong guard that no attempt was made. They are now in jail.

The Allegation and the Alligators.

NASHVILLE, February 16.—Representative Davis, who has been charged with having been bribed to vote for Republican candidates for secretary of state and comptroller, will publish a sworn statement in the American to-morrow morning, in which he denounces the allegations as false, and the testimony of witnesses before the legislative investigating committee as untrue.

Have Turned State's Evidence.

NASHVILLE, February 16.—Two negroes implicated in the Laprade murder turned State's evidence against the remaining five, who are on trial at Springfield, to-day, and testified there were ten in the party who went to murder Laprade for money he was supposed to have in his possession. Jack Bell was the leader of the gang. Anthony Duffy gave a most horrible account of the brutal treatment of Laprade, whom they cut and slashed, knocking his teeth out and breaking his skull, while he begged for mercy but to no avail.

ATTEMPT AT LYNCH LAW.
NASHVILLE, Feb. 17.—An effort was made last night to lyneh Tish and John Poe, in the jail at Winchester, charged with the murder of young Baker last week. A crowd of men boarded the train at Tullahoma to go to Winchester, but the conductor held the train. Fears are entertained that the effort will be repeated to night. The Governor has received a telegram from Judge Williams at Winchester, saying that a preliminary examination of the two Poes for the murder of Baker will be held to morrow morning. If the charge is proven, which is thought probable, they will be lynched. The Governor has ordered twenty men from the Porter Rifles and twenty from the Rock City Guards to go to Winchester to morrow morning.

Special to the Appeal.

SPRINGFIELD, TENN., February 17.—The evidence in the case of the LaPrade murderers closed this afternoon with the testimony of fifteen witnesses for the defense. Bill Murphy, one of the gang, was to have been brought on the stand. When he was informed when placed in jail here that the mob was to come that night and lynch him, he attempted to kill himself by butting his head against a stone wall, from which he has not yet recovered. The verdict will be rendered to-morrow. The statements of Duffy and Murphy agree with those made by Higgins, Bell and Jamison, when the last two named were lynched in September.

A Mob Disappointed.

Special to the Appeal.

WINCHERSTER, TENN., February 17.—Eighten men came to the jail this morning and demanded Fish and John Poe, but on the guards refusing to give them up they went away. The Poes were discovered as the burglars and murderers in having left a part of the bridle-reins which they had cut behind them. One of them, besides, had on clothing which was identified. The Poes were in the store robbing it when Baker, the murdered man, and his friend, Ball, rode up, having been to a wedding. The Poes, on being hailed, rushed out and commenced firing upon Baker and Ball.

The Object of Their Visit.

THE OBJECT OF THEIR VISIT.

NASHVILLE, February 17.—The object of the military being sent to Winchester to tomorrow morning is to bring the Poe murderers to the Nashville jail after their preliminary trial.

Bound to See the Show.

NASHVILLE, February 17.—An invitation to the legislature to be present at the inauguration of Garfield was adopted by that body, and nearly every member will leave here on the night of March 2d for Washington.

Troops Ordered to Winchester.

NASHVILLE, February 17.—The governor has received a telegram from Judge Williams, at Winchester, saying: "The preliminary examination of the two negroes for the murder of Baker will be held to-morrow morning. If the charge is proven, which is thought probable, they will be lynched. The sheriff at this time is absent summoning witnesses. Send him at least forty men to-night. The excitement is high, and it is doubtful if he can get a sufficient posse. No danger is apprehended before the examination, but afterward." The governor ordered twenty men from the Porter Rifles and twenty from the Rock City Guards to Winchester to-morrow morning.

SNOWED UNDER AGAIN.

Chicago Smothered Beneath a Five-Inch Fall of Snow.

CHICAGO, February 17.—Since 8 o'clock this evening nearly five inches of snow has fallen, and it is still coming down at the rate of an inch or two an hour. It is very compact, and lies where it falls, and will prove a great hindrance to railroad and foot travel. Coming as it does upon the heavy snows which have covered the ground almost without interruption since the middle of last November, this heavy fall of snow is quite remarkable and noteworthy. The air is cold and rawish, with no signs of a thaw.

THE OLD DOMINION.

Through the Democracy, Makes an Appeal for Homest Government.

RICHMOND, February 17.—The Conservative Democratic State central committee have called a convention at this city for August 4th next. An address has been is used giving a brief history of the organization of the party. It says: "What Republican triumph in southern commonwealths means let the wretched record of fifteen years attest. It signifies, in a word, the dethronement of the virtue, character, intelligence and prosperity of the State and the erection on their ruins of a dynasty of profligacy, ignorance and malice, whose unvarying fruits in the southern States have been social degradation, universal robbery and continued disorders."

The Nashville American, in two issues, lubricates its pen with mob oil to show that but for the presence in Winchester of "citizen soldiery," there would have been serious trouble and we would have deplored it. In fact, the American, in one article, thinks our action here is not civilization, enlightenment, or progress; in another article, wants to know if the people of Tennessee are mad, that they allow mob law to usurp the place of the Courts, and scoffs the idea of Winchester making a demand for a special term of Court to try the Poes. In this article says we are developing a state of society which will be insupportable. To this we reply that the Amerioan wholly misunderstands the late situation in Franklin county. There were no mob men here. There was a deep feeling of insecurity, consequent upon the fact that one of the prisoners was a man of a dare-devil spirit, who, already, wao under indictment for murder, and who had escaped from the iron cage in our brick jail, and for two or three years had escaped arrest. He had baffled the law, and his freedom was as if a mad dog or wild beast were allowed to roam at will. If there is a single person in this county who has expressed the opinion that the Poes were innocent, we are unaware of it. But the people (too often called a mob,) did not want anything but a speedy trial. They were tired of great criminals always bafflling the law. They did not want to pay immense sums of money just because, for a paltry fee, those criminals might get a shrewd attorney to stave off their trial from Court to Court, and, perchance, in the meantime the criminal escape again to murder and rob ad libitum. We tell the American, the people of Franklin county are not for mob law. All your moral lectures are as much deserved by the people of any other county in the State, if deserved at all. You speak from a high standpoint, but your premises are all wrong. You cannot commit a whole county to prison, and we tell you, if there is not more speedy justice in the Courts, this mockery of Justice called LAW will have to give way to the makers of the law—the People. The people of Franklin county never yet hung a man unjustly, but, perhaps, me-

The claimants of the Hyde estate seem to have come to grief—or rather to have been chasing a flickering will-o'-the-wisp, which has now escaped them altogether. The belts had organized an association for the purpose of employing lawyers to root out the estate from its supposed hiding place in the English Court of Chancery. The New York Sun contains a long story of the work of Hon. Thomas A. Logan, of Cincinnati, who was sent to England by the Hamilton county beirs to hunt up the estate. Mr. Logan has submitted his report, in which, after stating that he was assured at the American consulate that there was no such estate, he goes on to relate his search for it, and says: "The whole field was untrodden. I found it a labyrinth which I was compelled to explore in darkness and ignorance, without a compass, and with obstructions and confusion on every side. I did it, nevertheless, and now that I have done so, I am reluctantly and regretfully forced to admit that all they told me was entirely correct, and that my search was unprofitable, although not useless. After weeks of conscientious and assiduous labor, under the most trying circumstances, I have thoroughly satisfied myself that there is no fund now in the Bank of England or the Court of Chancery in the name of Hyde, or belonging by descent to any member of the various Hyde associations." In closing his report Mr. Logan says: "To show how successfully this business of claiming large estates is carried on, I would state that while I was in England another American lawyer arrived there to claim another estate valued at about three hundred millions of dollars; there was also an English association existing to recover another equal amount, and upon my arrival here, in the first newspaper I saw, was an announcement concerning another supposed estate, about equal in amount and in similar circumstances to yours and the others. It is evident at once that the sums claimed for recovery in these cases would alone bankrupt any nation on earth. While my mission has not been productive of pecuniary profit yet I think the result has been beneficial. It may now be definitely taken as a fixed fact that the so-called 'Hyde fund' does not exist, except in the fiction of traditions and the hopes of the expectant recipients. It was worth, however, much more than the personal outlay incurred by the individual members of this association to have settled once for all, in an authoritative manner, such a perplexing and delusive anticipation. And what is true of the Hyde fund may be asserted generally to be true of all the similar funds, trusts and estates, which are periodically advertised in this country, and which are kept before the public for the sole benefit of pecuniary speculators."

What the Poes Say.
A communication to the American, written in jail, yesterday, and signed by C. J. and John Poe, accused of the murder of Baker, in Franklin county, states that the charges made by "Justice" and published in yesterday's American are untrue. They say that neither of them ever went over the countries committing robberies, and the charge upon which they are now arrested is the first ever made against them in Franklin or any other county.

As to the intentions of the mob, they refer for proof to the officers of the Porter Rifles or Rock City Guards, and the Sheriff of the County. They think the object of "Justice" is to get them back to Winchester without a guard, and they fear that they will be lynched. They say that they will be acquitted of the murder of Baker if given a fair and impartial trial.

Continuing, the communication says:

I, John Poe, returned home the 12th day of December, 1879, and since that time I have molested no one, and have strictly obeyed the laws of Tennessee. I have never carried arms. I had nothing when I returned home but a Winchester rifle, which I left at Mrs. Steve Whitson's for six months.

I, C. J. Poe, landed at Blake Poe's, my uncle's, Dec. 2, 1880, and it is rumored that I broke jail in Texas and fled to Tennessee. I will just make this statement—that you or any other man can write to Austin, Henry Grove, Colville, Cook county, or Henrietta, Texas, for my character, and that will prove things for me.

A large number of witnesses—about 40, including both sides—were examined, which occupied the time of the Court until 5 o'clock Thursday evening, the 14th, and in two hours afterward (7 o'clock) the argument was opened by the Attorney-General with a two hours' speech. He was followed by Messrs. W. E. Colyar and P. R. Curtis, counsel for the defendants.
Friday morning Capt. T. D. Gregory spoke in behalf of the State, closing just before noon, and the afternoon was consumed by Messrs. John Simmons and Jesse Arledge, defendants' counsel.

Gov. Marks, for the State, made the closing argument. He commenced at 7 o'clock Friday night, and spoke till 9:30, when Judge Williams charged the jury, and the Court adjourned till next morning.

Saturday morning the jury appeared and requested that Judge Williams give further explanation in regard to the charge. The Judge said the only explanation he could make would be to re-read the charge, which he did in his usual articulate style, when the jury retired to their room in the Ballard House. This was about 10 o'clock.

At 1:30 p. m. the jury returned to the Court-room and rendered a verdict: Guilty of murder in the first degree. The counsel for defendants moved for a new hearing, and Court adjourned till Monday morning.

At 9 o'clock Monday morning Court was called. The movement of defendants' counsel for a new hearing was over-ruled. Judge W. then remarked that he was about to perform one of the most solemn duties of his life, and asked the prisoners if they had anything to say before sentence was passed upon them. John Poe raised to his feet and said that they had not been given a fair trial, that prejudice was high against them, that evidence had been produced which was untrue, that he could have produced witnesses whose testimony would have been valuable to them if he had been given time, &c. He then took his seat, and the death sentence was pronounced. Judge Williams said:

"It is the judgment of the Court that you, John Poe and Cicero Poe, be delivered to the Sheriff of Franklin county, to be put and kept in the jail of said county until Friday, the 17th day of June, 1881, and from thence taken by said Sheriff to a gallows within one mile of the Courthouse of Winchester, there to be hanged, each and severally, until you are dead. Said Sheriff shall erect said gallows and said defendants shall pay the costs of this prosecution."

After the sentence was passed, John Poe said, very audibly: "I guess I won't be at that scaffold."

The case was appealed to the Supreme Court, and at 11:30 o'clock Sheriff Turner, with a sufficient guard, left for Nashville with the prisoners, where they will remain until their case is acted upon by the Supreme Court, which meets next December. If the lower Court has erred in the trial they will get a new hearing; if to the contrary, the death sentence will be confirmed and another day be set by that body for their execution.

The Court adjourned about 11 o'clock, and Judge Williams left for Spencer to hold Court for the balance of the week. He will return and hold a special term here next week, commencing on Monday, for the purpose of trying those cases on the felony docket which were not continued.

We do not give the testimony of the witnesses in this trial, because we did not hear it all, other and more important business requiring our attention. It is enough to say, however, that, so far as our knowledge goes, the prisoners were given a fair and impartial trial, and the testimony produced against them corroborated what we printed at the time of their arrest; and, furthermore, the verdict accords, almost universally, with the views of the hundreds of persons who were present during the trial.

presidents-island-workhouse-1881-03.A3:
FOUL AND FILTHY Is the Condition of the President's Island Workhouse, According to the Committee of the County Court Which Reported to that Body Yesterday. The Bedding and Clothing of the Prisoners in an Indiscribable Condition, and the Air of the Sleeping Rooms Nasty Beyond Words to Tell.
The county quarterly court met for the April term at the courthouse yesterday morning, the following magistrates being present: Messrs. Dickason, Murray, Hunter, Williams, Hammontree, Hines, Moffet, Spelman, Quigley, Winters, Alexander, Coleman, Herring, Gowan, Pulliam, Kimbrough, Jones, Wellborn, Fletcher, Bledsoe, Harrell, Brett, Holman, Cole, Smith, Elliott, Fleming, Jennings, Mason, Stone and Elam.

GENERAL BUSINESS.

The following business was transacted: A number of petitions for reduction of assessments were granted; also a number of bills were allowed. The amount of $125 was ordered paid for building the bridge across Griffin creek, north of the new Brownsville road.

ELECTION OF ASSESSORS POSTPONED.

The election of city and county assessors was postponed until Monday, April 12th.

COUNTY WORKHOUSE.

The following report on Presidents Island county workhouse by the committee, consisting of Esquires Wellborn, Smith, Winters and Brett, was received and filed, and the court ordered that the committee be continued and that Chairman Holman and County-Attorney Taylor be added to it, and that Judge Horrigan and Attorney-General Turner, of the criminal court, be requested to act with them.

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE.

The committee visited the island workhouse on the 28th of March, arriving at noon, when the prisoners were at their noon meal.

A WORKHOUSE DINNER.

The allowance was placed on a tin plate for each prisoner. It consisted of a large square of cornbread, a heaped plate of cracked hominy, a large slice or rasher of pork, all well cooked and cleanly prepared. This was the kind and quantity of food prepared for the three daily meals, except at breakfast, when coffee was added, and at supper sometimes molasses was added. No charge of neglect as to food can be sustained.

BEDS AND BEDDING.

The whites, blacks and the women are separately confined at night. The bunks are arranged in three tiers. On the beds is a shuck mattress, a coarse osnaburg sheet, and on some one and on others two large, heavy woolen blankets.

WRETCHEDLY FILTHY.

In the room occupied by the negroes the bedding was wretchedly filthy, the sheets and ticking of the mattresses being begrimmed with grease and dirt. The committee could not learn when the bed-ticks had been washed, but the sheets had been washed soon after last Christmas. The room was very close, with unclean beds and unclean occupants.

A FOUL PRIVY.

The privy is not what it should be. It should be cut off or excluded by some means from the prison-room; now it occupies a prominent place in one end of the room, it being a platform raised high for a barrel from an opening on the outside, on top of the barrel being a large funnel. Taken in all surroundings it gave out an odor quite sickening to unaccustomed olfactoryes. If continued it must become very unhealthy during this spring and summer. The same objection can be made to the wards for whites and for women, but in these two latter wards the bedding was reasonably clean.

DIRTY PRISONERS.

In person the negro prisoners, particularly, and most of the whites, were unmitigating dirty. They did not know how long it had been since they had changed their clothing, and their dirty appearance was fair evidence of the truth of this charge; yet their clothing was not ragged.

TREATMENT OF PRISONERS.

The committee examined several prisoners as to their treatment, and offered the following cases as examples:

JOHN JONES'S STATEMENT.

John Jones, colored, was tound sick in his bunk; said he had been on the island two weeks; had been confined with piles since his arrival; had received no medical attention during that time except from Mr. Foster, one of the guards. He was unable to eat the food given him, and on complaint to Deputy Sheriff Collins he jabbed him in the sides, and hit him on the head with an iron poker, and also struck him on the head with a pistol, which, he said, was witnessed by many colored prisoners, and these prisoners so testified before the committee; yet the committee found but a small scab on the prisoner's head, which he said was made by the blow from the pistol.

STATEMENT OF HENRY EPPES.

Henry Eppes said he had been whipped by Lockery with a barrel stave without cause.

ARCHIE TINDALL TESTIFIES.

Tindall said he was whipped by Deputy Sheriff Collins because he was afraid to sit up with a sick man as directed by Collins; and he saw Mr. Stinson whip Robert Butler and Henry Eppes, striking them with his fist and with sticks.

DID NOT SEE IT.

Anthony Sexton said he had seen no persons whipped since he had been there, about ten days, but he did not stay in the colored ward.

REMARKS BY THE COMMITTEE.

The committee presents this summary of evidence on the subject of discipline or treatment; it is necessarily incomplete, it being the testimony of colored prisoners, except the last witness who had been only ten days on the island; the white prisoners being at work in a distant part of the field.

LITTLE MEDICAL ATTENTION.

The committee found one convict very sick, dangerously so, with pneumonia, and in the hospital. He said he had been sick three weeks, and in that time Dr. Willeford had been but once to see him; that he had very little attention paid to him.

THEY SAID THAT HE SAID.

It is due, however, to Deputy Collins to say that he and Mr. Stinson said that it was the duty of the guard to give attention to the sick, and that although Dr. Willeford had but once been to see the sick man, yet Mr. Foster, one of the employees on the island, had studied medicine, was a pretty fair doctor, and prescribed all necessary medicines, and that the sick man's wife lived near on the island, and was with him every day.

CONCLUDING REFLECTIONS.

The committee winds up the report by stating: "These are simply the facts as seen and heard by your committee, and as the members of that committee have each drawn a separate conclusion or inference upon which they might probably not agree, we tender no advice drawn thereform."

THE ISLAND BELOW.
Report of the Committee Appointed to Investigate.
The committee appointed to report upon the condition of the county workhouse on President island, composed of Esquires A. C. Welborn, C. E. Smith, P. M. Winters and James Brett, reported yesterday to the county court. The food they found good as to quantity and quality, but the beds in many of the wards filthy beyond all description. The sheets were washed last Christmas, but not since. A sickening odor pervaded the entire establishment. The prisoners wore whole clothes, but had not changed as far back as they could remember. John Jones, colored, was found sick in bed and stated that he was unable to eat the food given him, and on complaint to Deputy Collins that official had jabbed him in the side and hit him over the head with a poker, and also struck him over the head with a pistol. This, he said, was witnessed by most of the colored prisoners, and was substantiated by those whom the committee subsequently examined.

Joseph Williams, formerly a convict, but now a guard, said he saw Dockery, a former guard, whip Butler, a prisoner, and strike Jim Rogers, also a prisoner, over the head with a navy six, and afterwards spank him with a board.

Charlie Marshall, colored, testified to having been beat with an iron poker by Deputy Collins, and as evidence showed a set of peeled knuckles.

Archie Tindall said he had been beat by the same gentleman, because he was afraid to sit up with a sick man. Want of attention to the sick was also complained of.
The committee were reappointed to make a new investigation and report. The chairman, count attorney and Judge Horrigan will be invited to go down next time with the committee.

Workhouse Investigation.
The committee appointed by the
Workhouse Investigation.
The committee appointed by the county court to investigate Presidents island report that though they are satisfied no cruel treatment of prisoners is practiced, yet a proper regard for cleanliness is not observed. Many of the prisoners were exceedingly filthy, both as to clothing and bedding. The food was well cooked and nutritious. They suggest that the vault be removed from the house and connected with it by a tunnel; that cheap spoons be furnished, sufficient medical attendance be provided for the sick, who should be separated from the others, and that an occasional change be made in the food.

Terrible Fate of a Young Girl in South Carolina, and Prompt Punishment of Her Assailants.

CHARLESTON, S. C., Jan. 19.—Miss Bessie Wertz, daughter of William Wertz, living near Prosperity, in Newberry county, this State, was brutally outraged and murdered Monday evening while going from her brother's house to her home. Two negroes, named Spearman and Fair, were arrested on suspicion and lodged in the guard house. They confessed their guilt, and last night a large body of men took them out to lynch them. Spearman was shot to death on the spot where the crime was committed. Fair made his escape, but was recaptured to-day and hanged near Prosperity by a crowd of whites and blacks. The victim was 22 years old and a beautiful and excellent young lady.
two-men-prosperity.A2:
THAT SOUTH CAROLINA LYNCHING. The Shooting and Hanging of Two Negroes for the Murder of a Young Woman.
PROSPERITY, S. C., Jan. 19.—As Miss Bettie Wertz was returning home on the evening of the 17th from her brother's she was assaulted by Dave Spearman and Sam Fair, colored employees of her father. She was then tied and gagged, and Dave and Sam went to Mr. Wertz's and ate supper. Afterward, returning to their victim, they again assaulted her, and then choked her to death. The body was carried about twenty yards and laid down by a footpath, where it was afterward found.

Yesterday morning Justice Wheeler held a coroner's inquest. Suspicion rested on the above-named men. Sam confessed that he knew the deed was to be done, but said that he was not a participant in the act. The men were put in the guard house, to be carried to jail today. Last night the guard house doors were forced open and Dave was taken to the spot where the deed was committed, and where, it is said, he confessed that he and Sam committed the murder. Dave was tied to a pine tree and shot. The infuriated party then returned to the guard house, took Sam out, shot him, and left him for dead.

After daylight the incensed people searched for the bodies, and found Sam at his mother's, in bed, suffering from several bullet wounds. He was brought to Prosperity, taken about one mile from the town, and hanged at 1 o'clock in the afternoon. Whites and blacks assisted at the work, and about 250 or 300 men were witnesses. The deed was contemplated nearly a year according to the confessions of the murderers.
two-men-prosperity.A11:
Lynch-Law the Higher Law.
the law is slow and uncertain, even where the proof of guilt is clear and popular sentiment quickens and sustains prosecutor and jury. For a crime such as that which was committed near Prosperity on Monday night, there must be the speediest and severest punishment that civilization will allow. Burning at the stake or chopping the offender into mincemeat were not too much. But death, uncompromised by torture, the lynching of the two negroes who killed Miss Werts. The action of the citizens needs no apology. In what they did they represented society at large, and were the exponents of a law that is older than governments, and more venerable than the constitutions of States.

We grant that even lynching may not prevent the commission of the worst offenses in a State where the lowest class is large, and is easily made uncontrollable. But if lynching will not cure the evil, it will mitigate it. Nothing less than lynching is of any avail at all. And if simple shooting or hanging will not do, some still harder death will be found.—News and Courier.

TIED HER TO A BUSH;
And went to Mr. Wertz's and attended to his business and at his supper, and then he and Sam returned together, and after they had both abused the poor girl, they killed her. Last night about 1 o'clock the Coroner's Court adjourned without a verdict. Trial Justice, A. H. Wheeler, had the prisoners safely placed in the guard house. He and others remained near some time, until the crowd had partially dispersed and the excitement had abated. Then, feeling they were secure, he went home, and left the key with a constable. Some time after 2 o'clock yesterday morning, the guard house was broken open and the prisoners taken out. Dave was found shot dead, this morning, tied to the pile tree he had concealed himself behind. Sam was found at home with the marks of four balls, making slight wounds. An immense crowd of infuriated citizens went to his house, and brought him back to Prosperity. The Trial Justice and the jurors demanded the prisoner, but the crowd refused to give him up. As the news spread the crowd increased, and became more infuriated, and rushed over Justice Wheeler, and took Sam to the suburbs of the town and hanged him. About five or six hundred people participated in the lynching. In the crowd were many colored men and women. It is said that when her murderers tied their victim to the bush, and left her to go to the house for supper, it was their intention to return, and, after fully satisfying their brutal appetites, to destroy all traces of their crimes.

BURNING THE GIRL'S BODY.

Something occurred, however, to cause them to change their plans. The affair in all its details is certainly the most horrible ever known in this State. It is said that two or three negro men were also implicated in the assault on Miss Wertz. If evidence is adduced before the trial justice to strengthen this belief the suspect ed parties will be called to a speedy account, and, if the indignant populace are satisfied that they are guilty, the same stern and inexorable justice meted out to Spearman and Fair will be their reward. The body of Miss Wertz was interred yesterday in the family burial ground on her father's plantation, near Prosperity. The exercises were unusually impressive. The attendance probably numbered some six or eight hundred, and came from almost every portion of Newberry and contiguous counties.

Among the mourners were several old family servants and the old colored woman who had nursed the girl whose young life came to such an unhappy end, from her infancy up to the time
Among the mourners were several old family servants and the old colored woman who had nursed the girl whose young life came to such an unhappy end, from her infancy up to the time she was left to go to a seminary, where she finished her education. Miss Wertz returned home from a fashionable seminary last summer, from which she graduated with distinguished honor. She was a decided blonde, rather above the medium height, delicately formed, with soft brown curls, which clustered about a classic forehead.— Her eyes were of the deepest blue.
two-men-prosperity.A14:
DIABOLICAL CRIME OF TWO NÉGROES.
Near Prosperity, in Newberry county, on the evening of the 17th instant, as Miss Bessie Werts, daughter of William Werts, was going home from her brother's, whom she had been visiting, she was assaulted by two negroes, Dave Spearman and Sam Fair, who, after effecting their fiendish purposes, tied her to a bush, first gagging her, and then went to Mr. Werts' and got their supper; afterwards, returning to their unfortunate victim and again committing acts of violence, they killed her by choking her. At the coroner's inquest, suspicion rested on the above named parties and they were arrested, and confession on the part of Sam first, and then Dave, confirmed these suspicions. They were then lodged in the guard house. On Tuesday night they were taken from the guard-house by the infuriatad populace. Sam was shot on the spot and left as being dead, but Dave was carried to the spot where the crime was committed, tied to a pine tree, and then shot. On returning, the crowd did not find Sam, and at once search was instituted. He was found at his mother's and brought back to Prosperity. He was then taken about one mile from town, where his own life paid for his hellish acts, the negroes assisting in the vindication of right.
The following particulars of the affair, as certained subsequent to the lynching, are furnished by a reporter for the News and Courier, who visited the scene of the outrage and telegraphed under date of last Thursday:

Miss Werts was greatly beloved in the neighborhood where she was well known and respected. Her father is a large farmer living about two miles from town. On Monday evening, Miss Werts proceeded on a visit to her brother, about a mile and a quarter from home. Dave Spearman and Sam Fair, the former a coal black negro and the latter a mulatto, each about 21 or 22, were employed on the place. Sam was ploughing in a field in sight of the house, Dave working near her path. Sam was seen from the house working in the field until supper time, Dave's position being hidden by the trees. At supper time both came to the house, ate supper in the kitchen under the observation of Mr. Werts, who spoke with them on various subjects, and did not see a trace of uneasiness about them. After supper they went out again for the night. Dave was married and lived with his wife on the place; Sam lived with his mother on an adjoining plantation, to reach which he would have to take the same path as the murdered girl.

Miss Werts did not return that night, but this excited no uneasiness, as it was supposed she had stayed with her brother. Next morning Sam went to Mr. Werts, considerably agitated, and told him his daughter was lying dead under a fence, about a half mile from the house. Mr. Werts hurried there, accompanied by Sam, and, on finding the dead body of his daughter, sent him to summon the neighbors, he waiting beside her. In going to the spot, Sam had accounted for her death by saying he thought Miss Bessie might have injured herself by falling over the fence. Neighbors and friends quickly gathered, and an immediate investigation was made, followed by the discovery of the perpetration of a hideous crime.

A coroner's jury met in Prosperity and several persons were examined, no clue being found to direct suspicion. Both the murderers were present as spectators. Here Mr. H. C. Moseley began some intelligent detective work. Having an indefinable suspicion of Sam's knowledge of the crime, he, in an indifferent manner, asked him to take off his coat and vest. He did so, and on minute examination of the latter a strand of wool was found near the lapel of the color of the fringe of Miss Werts' shawl and a hair of the color of hers near it. He became very nervous at this, and was taken aside and rigidly interrogated. Little by little he furnished the following statement to the jury:

He and Dave, he said, had projected their crime since last spring. Dave had told him that he intended to meet Miss Bessie that evening, and asked him to join him. He refused, and endeavored to persuade him from it. Dave had told him that night he was afraid that, after his treatment of that young lady, she was dead, and had asked him to take another path home than the one the body was found on to go home on, as there was somebody on the other. He and Dave went by the other path and separated, Dave returning to his wife, and he going to his mother's house. He acknowledged that the next morning he had told his stepfather that Miss Werts was not at home the night before, although he had left home at dark and couldn't know other than by participation in the crime. He and his stepfather had gone to the spot on Tuesday morning, being told by a negro that he had seen some one lying by the road in the night, and he there found
two-men-prosperity.A15:
have been her lying there from her clothes.

Dave and Sam were then confronted in the court room before the jury, but Dave denied every allegation of the other negro. They were then placed in the guard-house, where Trial Justice A. H. Wheeler had provided a guard, and the jury, after sitting until 1 o'clock Wednesday morning, without a verdict, adjourned to 1 P. M.

A large crowd had listened to the revelations of Sam with intense indignation and horror, and after the adjournment of the jury proceeded to the guard-house, overpowered the guard, cut down the door and took Dave out, leaving Sam within, not having proof against him. The night was rainy and dark. A mass of men, among whom were a number of negroes, swept rapidly along with the doer of this horrible deed towards the place of its committal. Arriving there, Dave made the following blood curdling confession:

He said he had laid in wait behind a large pine tree till Miss Werts returned from her visit. As she passed him on the path, he sprang behind her and seized her by the shoulders. She entreated him piteously to let her go, promising everything in the world she had if he would. He choked her until insensible, tied a rag (afterwards found to be Sam's handkerchief) tightly around her neck, knotted it firmly to a sapling and accomplished his infamy. He went to the house and after supper returned with Sam. They found her still breathing. Sam then outraged her, he standing by. Sam then choked her to death for fear she would inform on them. They then removed the body about forty yards, throwing it in the path just beneath the fence. He told where he had buried the rag he had used to tie her, and this was identified by Sam's family as belonging to him.

This ghastly and almost incredible tale, told in the forest glade which had witnessed its origin, moved his captors to frenzy. Many were for burning him alive, but more moderate counsels prevailed. He was tied by the neck and waist to the pine tree where he had lurked in waiting for his victim, and about 4 o'clock in the morning, while the sweeping rain fell heavily, a dozen guns flashed out of the darkness and ended as monstrous a story as ever reached human ken. The negro was indifferent and cool to the last, avering his willingness to die, and betraying no fear.

The party returned to Prosperity, where they took Sam out of the guardhouse and poured a volley into him, leaving him for a corpse. They then dispersed. Later in the morning it was ascertained that he had slipped away and reached his mother's house, about three miles distant. During the day the coroner's jury had rendered the verdict already telegraphed. A strong party went in search of him, and found him in bed suffering from several slight wounds which were pronounced not dangerous by the physicians. He was taken to Prosperity in a buggy under escort, and for an hour or two a consultation was held as to his disposition.
About midday the crowd escorted the wretch, who walked willingly to a pine grove about half a mile from the town. He declined to say anything more than he had already done. He was led to a stoutly branched pine tree, a noose put round his neck and an agile negro climbed the tree and passed the rope over a limb. Every one grasped it, and the second of the fiends suffered the vengeance of an outraged people. The lynchers then gradually and quietly dispersed with hardly a dissenting voice against the primitive but trustworthy justice they had meted out.

The funeral procession of Miss Werts had only preceded this procession of vengeance on the same road by half an hour.

The dead bodies of the fiends who perpetrated the diabolical deed, and who suffered a just and merited punishment, remained several days without sepulture. The authorities of the colored church in that neighborhood refused permission to bury them in their grave-yard, and the negroes refusing to bury the body of Sam Fair, two gentlemen of Newberry secured his burial on Saturday at their own expense.

Miss Werts was the only unmarried daughter of her father, and was possessed of considerable property. She was engaged, and was to have been been married in March to a gentleman residing at present in Charleston.
two-men-prosperity.A18:
A Woman Hanged by a Mob in Laurens County.
The habit of lynching weak and defenceless negroes in this State has gone on constantly for several years, and without censure, but now we are glad to see that two or three journals of the State have had the manhood to denounce the recent hanging of the half-witted negro woman in Laurens county.—Abbeville Press and Banner.

The hanging of this woman by a mob can not be too severely condemned, and we trust the officers of the law in Laurens County will ferret out the guilty parties and have them punished according to the enormity of their crime. The zeal of our esteemed contemporary in this direction is to be commended, but when it accuses the people of the State of "the habit of lynching weak and defeseless negroes," we think it is going farther than the facts will justify. The only lynching in the State that we remember, up to the time of the lynching of this woman, was for the heinous offense of rape and murder. The first fiend who met the vengeance of an outraged community for rape, was John J. Moore, a white man in Spartanburg county. Then followed the lynching of three negroes in Clarendon county for the brutal murder of a white woman and plundering of the house, and the lynching of the two negro brutes at Prosperity for the outrage and murder of Miss Wertz.

The indiscrtminate charge of murder and lawlessness against our people is common with the Radical sheets of the North, but the Press and Banner is the first Democratic paper in the State, or the South, which has made a similar charge. It would have been better for the good reputation of our contemporary to have given the number of "weak and defenseless negroes" lynched, and the character of the offenses for which they were lynched. If it had persued this course and then given its unqualified condemnation of the persons who committed the deeds and the papers who commended them, there would have been some consistency in its course, but when it makes a wholesale charge against the people of the State without giving the number of "weak and defenseless" negroes lynched, and the character of their offenses, we think it is placing itself in a very unenviable position to say the least of it. No doubt its assertion will be copied by all the bloody shirt organs of the North, and quoted upon every political rostrom by Republican speakers, as the highest Democratic evidence that their charges against the white people of the South are true. Such reckless and unjust charges are calculated to do us more harm than the treachery of all the Mahonns in the South.

Southern cotton mills have made money while their Northern rivals were being satisfied at holding their own. After such experience perhaps the South will turn her hand to other industries, the raw material of which she has in abundance. There would be more money in it than in politics and more honor too.—N. Y. Herald. We will attend to both little matters thank you.

CRIMES AND CASUALTIES-BY TELEGRAPH.
A MESSENGER BURNED TO DEATH.
PHILADELPHIA, Nov. 5. — Edward Burke, an American District Telegraph messenger, was burned to death this morning by the explosion of an oil lamp at the office at Broad and Chestnut-sts.

硫酸TED WITH A RAZOR.
BANGOR, Me., Nov. 5. — Charles R. Lewis, a negro, was arrested last night for assaulting John Nolan with a razor. Nolan identified him as his assailant, but Lewis denies all knowledge of the crime.

MORTALLY WOUNDED BY A NEGRO.
ATLANTA, Ga., Nov., 5. — A dispatch to The Constitution from Camak, Ga., says: "At a negro 'supper' near here a drunken negro shot and mortally wounded Elias Edwards, a respectable white citizen."

KILLED WHILE OUT HUNTING.
NEW-BRUNSWICK, Nov. 7. — Walter Seabring killed Henry Waters to-day, at Hope Villa, Madison Township, by the accidental discharge of his gun. He was out hunting, and while loading his gun, the hammer fell and the discharge entered Walter's brain.

KILLED IN RESISTING A SHERIFF.
LITTLE ROCK, Nov. 5. — Felix Burke, a negro, was killed yesterday, in Monroe County, by Deputy-Sheriff McDonald who was endeavoring to arrest him for stealing a male. A fierce pistol light occurred between the men, and McDonald was dangerously wounded.

A STUDENT MURDERER.

TIEPIN, O., November 5.—The preliminary trial of Charles Madder, a student, who murdered Miss Phoebe Bernard on Thursday night, because she declined to marry him, is in progress. A great deal of excitement is manifested, and fears are entertained that if the result of the trial is not satisfactory, Madder will be lynched.

KICKED TO DEATH.

AUGUSTA, Ga., November 5.—Last night two colored men named James Barnett and Moses Martin had a difficulty. They engaged in a hand-to-hand struggle and Martin kicked Burnett to death.

NOT GUILTY.

NAPOLEON, Ohio, November 6.—At 11 a. m. the jury in the Gev. Scott murder case returned a verdict of not guilty.

A MULE THIEF KILLED.

CINCINNATI, November 6.—Little Rock special says that Deputy Sheriff McDonald shot and killed Felix Burell, a mule thief, during a running fight in Monroe county yesterday and McDonald was badly wounded. Burell stole a mule from a widow two months ago and yesterday came back and stole another.

TRAN MEN INDICTED.

SANFORD, Ky, November 6.—L. F. McNama, conductor, and Wm Taite, engineer of the train, that killed five men at McKinney, on the Cincinnati Southern Railway two weeks ago, have been indicted for murder in the first degree. They ran off immediately after the collision and have not since been heard of. The Governor will offer a reward for their capture.

SENTENCED TO BE HUNG.

JERSEY CITY, N. J., November 6.—Kanskowski, who murdered Mina Muller, was to-day sentenced to be hanged on January 6th, 1882. When asked if he had anything to say why sentence of death should not be pro-
changed on January 6th, 1882. When asked if he had anything to say why sentence of death should not be pronounced upon him he said "God knows that since this court house was built no more innocent man has been within it, God knows this." After sentence had been pronounced he exclaimed, "God knows I am innocent."

A ROW IN CAMP.

COLUMBUS, Ga., November 6.—In the camp of Mr. English, on the P. & Railroad in Florida, a white man named Turnage and a colored man named Quinley engaged in an altercation. The other negroes took it up and at night fired into the camp, resulting in the death of a colored man and the wounding of other parties.

ROW AT A DANCE.

ATLANTA, Ga., November 6.—Several white men went to a negro dance near Carmad last night and got into drunken row with some negroes. Elias Edwards (white) was shot in the temple by Austin Howard, a negro, and killed. Another white man was not though not fatally. The negro escaped.
